speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege I desire to point out that on Friday last I directed attention to the fact that the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) had given certain warnings at his nomination convention. I did that on the strength of a statement that said the warning was given and indicated that he had used the language at his nomination meeting. I have since investigated the matter with great care, and I find that the Winnipeg Free Press of October 22, and the Winnipeg Tribune of the same day, make reference to his nomination. It was incorrect for me to say that the hon. member for St. Boniface had made the statement in question. It was made by the president of the Liberal Association of Manitoba. I quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of October 22:
John Caswell Davis, president o.f the Manitoba Liberal Association', warned that the Conservatives probably would introduce a "false issue" into the campaign to separate the people of the dominion on a racial and nationality basis.
That is all that is said. The report in the Tribune is this:
Referring to the Stevens commission, J. C. Davis, president of the Provincial Liberal Association, stated that, so far, only "handpicked" concerns had been investigated. The "big fellows" were still untouched. He also warned the electors against possible attempts on the part of the Conservative government to so juggle amendments to the British North America Act as to stir up racial feeling.
I express my very sincere regrets that I did an injustice to the hon. gentleman on Friday last when, in consequence of the dispatch to which I had reference-which was neither one of these-not mentioning who was responsible for the statement, I attributed the statement to him. That was an error and I offer him my apologies for having done so. But the statements in question were made by the president of the Liberal association in the province of Manitoba, who was speaking presumably in the presence of the hon. gentleman.
I have nothing to say in the matter, and I appreciate the Prime Minister's action in this regard.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF RAILWAY FROM DISTRICT TO PACIFIC COAST

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. KENNEDY (Peace River) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF RAILWAY FROM DISTRICT TO PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Peace River country should be connected by a direct railway outlet to the Pacific coast.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I introduced a similar resolution on the last day of February, last session. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) at that time moved an amendment to the resolution making it read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Peace River country should be connected by a direct outlet to the Pacific coast when circumstances permit.
He commented as follows:
This amendment is not moved with any desire of blocking the resolution, but rather to call attention to the necessities of the present financial situation. ... I suggest therefore that the hon. gentleman accept the amendment on the understanding that it means exactly what it says; that when circumstances permit, which we trust will be in the very near future, every consideration will be given this project.
Throughout the year we have had I believe a very general improvement in Canada, in Great Britain, in other countries of the empire and also in the United States. It is only a few months ago that in the United States the recovery program was endorsed by an overwhelming majority, showing, I think,

Peace River Outlet
that in the opinion of the vast majority there had been a distinct improvement in that country. A few days ago I read in the press a statement coming apparently from the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin in which he was reported to have said that Britain was leading the world in recovery. Of course we had the radio addresses of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) assuring us that the ship of state was well through the storm and that the time for definite action toward permanent reform hau come. There is no doubt that anyone who is conversant with price levels, farm prices, railway freight conditions, railway earnings and even I think unemployment figures, will concede, whatever opinions he may have about the system under which we are living, that there has been a very definite improvement in the last twelve months.
I want to say a word about the form of my resolution. I have always introduced this resolution in pretty much the form in which I am introducing it to-day, but the Peace River railway problem is not merely one of an outlet; it is an outlet with the necessary connections within the country itself. It is a problem comprising some mileage that might be considered main line and a large percentage of branch lines that will serve local territory throughout the Peace River country. Sir Henry Thornton appearing before the Duff commission in 1931-32 made the statement that in his opinion that commission was appointed about thirty years too late; in other words it was appointed to try to straighten up certain troubles that had developed in connection with the railways of this country instead of having been appointed thirty years ago when it might have prevented a number of these troubles from developing. The Peace River did have its investigation at the beginning of the thirty years and not at the end, and in 1927 a very complete survey of the Peace River country as a whole was made with reference to the 10,000,000 acres suitable for settlement and readily available. I think it may be said that the plan was studied with a view to serving that whole territory, gradually building up the railway system and providing ultimately for over 1,000 miles of railway without one mile of duplication. We have railway unification in the Peace River because the Peace River railways are to-day jointly owned, so I do not think it can be said that we are going to have any troubles from duplication such as exists in the rest of Canada.
Whenever we speak about railway development the natural tendency seems to be to
bring up this question of the railway problem. What is the railway problem of Canada? It has been exhaustively studied by commission after commission and by railway experts, but I do not think that anywhere has it been suggested that either in the interests of the railways themselves or in the interest of the country generally branch lines properly laid out are anything but an asset. So I am going to argue that branch lines, or any railway that may serve local territory suitable for settlement and already settled, cannot be any part of Canada's railway problem. In the Dray-ton-Acworth report of 1917, in section 7 of the summary of conclusions and recommendations, I find the following;
The development of Canada justified two transcontinental lines. It did' not justify three. The Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern should have been amalgamated.
There is no suggestion throughout the Drayton-Acworth report that branch lines properly built and properly located had anything to do with creating the railway problem of Canada.
Then we have the Duff commission report, which goes into this matter somewhat extensively and from which I wish to make a few quotations. At page 41, dealing with the duplication of railway mileage it says:
The duplication of railway mileage in Canada is of two general types:-
(a)	the lines of railway constructed by various owners, which lines, when they came under common ownership and operation, were found to a considerable extent to be duplicative of one another;
(b)	the directly competitive sections of the two principal systems which, because of unwise rivalry and lack of cooperative spirit, were separately constructed, whereas joint construction and operation, or agreement as to running rights over lines already constructed, would have served' all necessary requirements and prevented much waste of public and private funds. Related to this group are lines which are functionally duplicate although not located in the same territory.
These problems relate to both branch and trunk lines. Of the lines in group (a) it has been possible, since the consolidation of the Canadian National system in 1923, to eliminate a certain amount of duplicate mileage.
It then refers to the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk between Edmonton and Red Pass Junction and between Napanee and Toronto. Then it continues:
The principal duplications of type (b) involve main line mileage of considerable length, with long-established services.
On page 19 we find this statement:
An outstanding feature of this large expenditure is the amount spent on branch lines.
Peace River Outlet

The two railways expended, during the nine year period, $162,451,546 in the construction and acquisition of branch lines totalling 5,018-60 miles. A policy of cooperation would have avoided a considerable part of this expenditure, probably one-third. This mileage is equivalent to the provision of a line of railway extending from Halifax to Vancouver and back again to the Manitoba boundary.
Then on page 21 it is said:
On behalf of the Canadian Pacific it was stated that the company had been forced to anticipate the building of branch lines, the construction of which might have been deferred without injury to the public, and that protective lines had had to be projected under a threat of invasion by the Canadian National.
The Canadian National stated that to refrain from branch line construction would result in 'the system being deprived of any opportunity for reasonable and proper development. Strategic territories, contiguous to their main lines, would be entered by their rival and, while admitting that they entered upon the construction of lines not immediately required, they defended this policy on the ground that to open up new territory in anticipation of settlement and immigration, and to maintain the company's relative position with regard to the rival transport enterprise, was in the long run justified.
The only criticism is with regard to duplication; duplication of branch lines and duplication of main lines, both in the Drayton-Acworth report of 1917 and the Duff commission report of 1932.
I have before me two speeches made by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. E. W. Beatty. In the speech made in Toronto on January 16, 1933, he said:
Canada has a population of about ten million people. It has approximately 42,000 miles of railway, or 236 people per mile of railway. In other words, it has fewer people per mile of railway than any other civilized country. It has several thousands of miles paralleled by other miles, serving the same territory and reaching the same terminals. This constitutes our greatest individual item of waste. Why should we maintain something we do not require and maintain it at tremendous loss, and can we afford to do so?
The point in all these statements is parallel lines; two railways being built where only one was required created the problem. I argue that inasmuch as in the Peace River country the projected lines have been located so that such a situation cannot arise, railway construction there should not be held up because of any recommendation that has ever been made to the House of Commons so far as I can see by any authority competent to speak on the matter. I am willing to admit that Mr. Loree did say something about lines having light traffic, but anyone who understands the railway situation in Canada knows that branch 
lines on the frontier are as necessary to main lines as are the branches or roots to the trunk of the tree. They act as feeders, without them the main lines would not have the traffic necessary to make them profitable. Mr. Beatty said in respect to branch lines that they are an asset to the railway as well as to the country, railway construction must proceed if a new country is to develop and progress. The only essential is to keep that construction within reasonable bounds, which are governed by economic principles and the application of intelligence.
I think I have made that point clear enough. One cannot study the history of railway development in Canada without being struck by the tremendous swing from increasing mileage by thousands of miles annually down to practically nothing. I have before me a statement showing the number of miles of new construction coming into operation each year since 1900. I see that in 1922 we had 3 miles, in 1915, we had 4,783 miles. The average for the thirty-four years from 1930 to 1933 was about 750 a year. It was true that the vast mileages built in one year were in what has been called periods of prosperity. But I think that railway construction, the investment of new capital, was a cause as well as a result of prosperity. It is very difficult to unscramble cause and effect in a matter of that kind.
When the depression struck Canada-and I am now coming to part of the financial side of my argument-the first reaction of governments and businesses everywhere was to economize by cutting out capital expenditure, but we very soon found out that this kind of economy was creating about as many problems as it was getting us away from. People refused to invest money; government estimates were cut down; public w'orks were not proceeded with. These were all temporary expedients, but there is not a government in Canada that has not been forced to review the problem in an altogether different way. In 1930 in this parliament we had a vote of $20,000,000 to provide for unemployment relief. Since that time I believe the government of this country has provided for the same purpose something like $111,000,000. Last year in this house we passed a bill providing $40,000,000 for the construction of public buildings. Within the last few days the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) introduced a resolution advocating a housing program in Canada, and I think the statement made by the Prime Minister in connection with that debate was very significant. The right hon. gentleman said that the purpose of

Peace River Outlet
a good deal of this sort of legislation was primarily to provide employment, and that the secondary effect would be to create other employment throughout the country.
In introducing this resolution this afternoon I want to say that in my judgment it can be viewed from the standpoint of the relief of unemployment and the provision of housing accommodation in the pioneer settlements of the Peace River district, and I think it is just as capable of being considered from that standpoint as from any other. The railway problem of Canada is related to the whole economic problem of the country, and it seems to me that if we can relieve unemployment by constructing public works, by investing public money or in other ways, and at the same time do work that is really necessary or that will be necessary in the very near future, we will be doing something really worth while. I believe the settlement of the Peace River country is permanent; I do not think there is a single thing about that country to indicate that in a short time it will be farmed out, or that it will be affected by drought or anything else that will drive settlers away. From my twenty-three years' experience in that country I can say that it has all the elements of permanency so far as weather and soil conditions are concerned. I do not believe you can have a permanent agriculture without live stock, and you cannot have live stock without suitable conditions to produce grass and feed. There is no place in the Peace River district, so far as I know, where these things cannot be grown, whether it is alfalfa, grain or any kind of grass. In that country we have timber, and I think the records for the last twenty-three years will show that the rainfall always has been ample. With all these advantages, together with the fact that ground fruits may be grown at any point, I think we can expect people to come there and make permanent homes in that district.
So, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I am asking the government seriously to consider commencing in the near future the construction of at least some railway mileage to serve that settlement which is already in existence. I am asking the government to build railways that will fit in wdth all the plans that have been worked out for an outlet to the Pacific coast and which, in the meantime, will serve a settlement that has all the elements of being permanent. To-day we have settlers trying to establish themselves twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty and eighty miles from the railway. A few years ago the Alberta government sent Doctor Wyatt, of the Alberta research council, to the Peace River country to make an intensive survey of soil conditions. He made
a survey of about 3,000,000 acres, and as a result we know that the soil is suitable for settlement. It is not all first class, but a very large proportion of it is. I should like to put on record the winnings of the farmers of the Peace River country at some of the big fairs during the last few years. I am quoting from the Grande Prairie Herald, old timers' historical section, issued about two months ago:
Eighteen World Championships Won at Chicago in Last Eight Years
Winning a total of thirteen championships in grain classes at the International Hay and Grain Show at Chicago within eight years, and in addition taking so long a list of first, second and third prizes in all classes of grains both at Chicago and at the Royal Winter Fair at Toronto and at other shows throughout Canada, farmers of the Grande Prairie district have succeeded in firmly establishing this district as the greatest grain growing area on the North American continent.
Championship wheat was first sent out of the Peace River country as far back as GO years ago, a priest of the mission at Fort Chipewyan won a world championship at Philadelphia with wheat grown in the mission garden at the far northern outpost. Again in 1893 the late Rev. Gough Brick captured the world championship at Chicago. Then for 17 years Canada did not appear in the list of big prize winners, and the Peace River country did not undertake competition until 1923, when Herman Trelle of Wembley, exhibiting for the first time, took third prize in spring wheat, and went back to Chicago in 1926 to win the double championship in both wheat and oats.
From that time onward, the Wembley district of the Peace River country has established itself firmly as the outstanding grain growing area of the continent, with a record of five world championships in wheat, five in oats, four in peas, two in timothy and one each in rye and flax. World champion grain growers of the Wembley district since 1926 include Herman Trelle, 13 championships: Erich Andersen, two; John Allsop, one, and P. U. Clubine, one, with Robert Cochrane, of Grande Prairie, taking one. The final bid for fame was made by Wembley grain growers this season, when three young members of the junior grain club, John Allsop, Paul Sebastian and Justyn Rigby captured respectively championship and third and fourth prizes in spring wheat class, 'while Herman Trelle took championship in oats. Others who have figured in world championships are Erich Andersen, former oat king, and Robert Cochrane, who has swept the board at Chicago in timothy seed, of which he was a few years ago classed as the largest producer on the continent.
I think this record shows that in the Peace River we have a country with very rich soil. I believe the yields in the Peace River country over a period of years have shown that the climate is proper for purposes of production. The records show that settlement is fairly well developed along the route of the proposed outlet, and that the railway would traverse a region as rich as any in western Canada. I have mentioned before and I
Peace River Outlet

should like to repeat that according to the surveys there would be 6,000 economic acres of land per mile of railway in the Peace River district, while there are only 5,000 in the rest of the prairie provinces.
What would be the significance of the construction of a certain mileage of railways, probably fifty or sixty or whatever it may be, from the standpoint of unemployment relief or that of enabling settlers to establish themselves? A purchasing power would be put into circulation which would affect not only steel rails, groceries or other commodities, but would have a tendency to keep in circulation the economic wealth of the dominion.
A good deal has been said as to whether or not branch lines pay, and in this connection the Northern Alberta Railways have been mentioned. I know that all railways in Canada are to-day having their difficulties.
Speaking before the Senate committee Mr. E. W. Beatty, chairman and president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company stated that the branch lines built by that railway were not losing any more money than were the main lines. I quote the following from Mr. Beatty's statement before the standing committee of the Senate on railways, telegraphs and harbours:
Industrial and commercial enterprises also entered new fields, and for all these, railway service was necessary. These settlements and industries owed their existence in a very large masure to the colonization and development work of the company, and it was but natural that it should look forward to a share of the traffic which they might yield. As has been said, the orderly progress of its program was affected by the action of the rival system, but the future of the company could not have been protected if it had refrained from following the march of settlement. The traffic returns of the new lines up to 1930 fully justified their construction, and the falling returns of subsequent years have been no more characteristic of the new lines than of other parts of the railway.
I have been preparing some figures in connection with operating ratios of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Northern Alberta Railways. It is not possible to take one comparison and be certain that one has been fair. I believe however that a comparison of operating ratios would be a fairly safe guide as to just what a railway is doing. Having in mind the fact that all railways find it difficult to earn not only operating but additional charges, I should like to place some figures on Hansard. I find that in 1933 the gross earnings per mile of railway of the Canadian Pacific Railway amounted to $6,111; on the Canadian National Railways it amounted to $5,700 and on the Northern Alberta Railways, $1,621. I do not believe we can have sensible and economic construction of railways by alternating between tremendous programs of construe-
tion and no construction. If we are to build railways economically we will have to do so gradually and steadily. Professor Jackman at page 30 of his book Economics of Transportation shows how the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway cost far more than was originally estimated bceause at the time of its construction there was an extensive construction program throughout Canada

Peace River Outlet
resulting in much higher costs for rails and material than had been originally estimated. That is inevitable if we are going to have booms and depressions. It seems to me the time has come when we ought to face our problems squarely, without fear, in the full belief that Canada must develop and that we must develop it steadily. It has been said if we cannot cut off the tops of the booms and the bottoms out of the depressions we can never have stabilization.
I believe the time has come when we must face the problem about which I have been speaking. In my judgment the Peace River country must be settled. Because of weather conditions in the southern part of the province settlers will be driven to the northern areas. The Peace River area is rich in natural resources, and in this connection we must not forget what the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) said last year about the resources west of the mountains as well as the fertile country to the east. As undoubtedly this railway will ultimately be built I believe we ought to start right now, because there is a need for additional purchasing power, and an opportunity would be afforded settlers who otherwise might be in the bread lines to establish themselves. The time has come for some action towards the building of at least lines which to-day may be branch lines but which would work into a permanent scheme for future railway service for the Peace River country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not purpose to cover the ground as thoroughly or from as wide a viewpoint as has the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy). He has, in fact, covered the situation so well from the general standpoint that I think it could not have been better done. There is one remark that he made during the course of his address with which I heartily agree, and that was that the government of this dominion, in providing for the relief of unemployment through the construction program which they have in mind would do well to provide work for these pioneers living on the outskirts of civilization so that they could maintain themselves without having to go on the dole. That is one very good reason I think why the construction of this railway would justify itself many times over.
My hon. friend from Peace River mentioned that there were people in the Peace River country who had to go sixty miles to get to a railroad, but in the British Columbia area of the Peace River I think my hon. friend knows perfectly well that there are many people living to-day who have to go a
great many more miles than sixty to get to a railway. As a matter of fact, some of the residents of the district that I have the honour to represent are attempting to produce crops and earn their livelihood as far as one hundred miles away from the railway.
There was another remark made by my hon. friend from Peace River with which I also fully agree, and that is that the construction and completion of this railway outlet for the Peace River country should be undertaken gradually and steadily. I am going to suggest that at least a start might be made on the construction of this railway to serve the people who are already located in the area and who are a great distance from the end of steel. That construction would be of very great benefit to these people. I refer to that part of the Peace River territory which lies on the north side of the Peace river and within the province of British Columbia.
In order that the general public may understand the situation may I say that the Peace River country, speaking generally, is about one thousand feet in elevation above the level of the Peace river, and that the people living north of the river in the British Columbia section of the Peace River territory have to haul ail their supplies and production from that height of land down one thousand feet to the level of the river, and then cross the river, and climb up again to the same height on the other side of the river. It must also be remembered that during at least two months of the year the river is impassable on account of ice conditions, when the ferries are not able to operate. I am going to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that those people who live on the north side of the river should be supplied with railway facilities at as early a date as possible.
The northern Alberta railway lines are at present built to a place called Hines Creek, and to reach the area which I have been speaking of you have to go about one hundred miles west of Hines Creek; and 150 miles from Hines Creek would bring the railway to Hudson Hope, to the canyon of the Peace river. I suggest that as a matter of unemployment relief it would be good business for the government to provide two or three million dollars to construct that part of the line from Hines Creek west to Hudson Hope, or as much of it as that amount of money would construct. I do not think that is asking a great deal from the government, and I think the government would find that it would be money very well spent, because it fits absolutely into the scheme as outlined
Peace River Outlet

by the hon. member for Peace River for the construction of the western outlet for the Peace River country. It would remain for all time as part of the main line of the western outlet., and let me remind the house and the country that both the government and the opposition are on record in favour of providing the Peace River country with a western outlet. To make a small start such as I have suggested would be a very good thing in times like these. In that area north of t'he Peace river we have a population at the present time of four thousand people; I am talking now altogether about the British Columbia end of the Peace River country. There are in the Peace River area of British Columbia a total of about ten thousand people, four thousand of whom are on the north side of the river, and who, as I have explained, have to transport their supplies and production from one side of the river to the other.

How many people would that branch that my hon. friend suggests serve?
Mr. FRASER (Cariboo); About four thousand people at the present time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to put on record some resolutions that I have received. The first is from the board of trade of Fort St. John, as follows:
Moved by Mr. Finch, seconded by Mr. Bruce: That in view of the fact there is no likelihood of a coast outlet in the near future and the district lying north of the Peace, being separated from the railroad by the said river, which for at least two months in the year is impassable and,
Whereas the majority of land lying between Fort St. John and Hines Creek is good agricultural land, and is in a district where a railroad could be built economically.
Therefore we respectfully urge that the railroad from Hines Creek, Alberta, be extended to the Beaton river, British Columbia, at the earliest possible date.
The Beaton river is in the centre of the area which I have described. Here is another communication from the Fort St. John Farmers' Institute, addressed to myself, under date of January 29:
Naturally we are very interested in a railway outlet for the country on the north side of the Peace river and we are writing you, respectfully requesting you to represent to the proper authorities the great need of this particular part of the country for better railway transportation.
As you are arvare, at present agricultural products must be taken by truck, on roads only fit for their use during part of the year, or by the much slower means of sleigh or wagon for a distance of about sixty miles to the

railhead at Dawson Creek. That is the distance from Fort St. John, it being considerably greater from other important parts of this large and fertile agricultural area. You of course also know that at certain times of the year it is not possible or practicable to get freight across the Peace river-this being a serious problem in the matter of delivery of farm produce to the railhead.
It has been stated that this country is not ripe for a railway and probably some estimate, in support of that contention, has been made of the freight at present available. Are the farmers expected to raise crops and stock to full capacity without really adequate means of shipping and with no hope of obtaining those facilities within a reasonable period? We think that this is a point that is often lost sight of. You of course have information at hand showing the extent and potentialities of this country and we are not forgetful of representations you have already made.
An extension of that branch of the N.A.R., which is on the North side of the Peace river, into what was known as the " Block," would, we think, greatly help the farmers on the north side by shortening their road haul.
Respectfully yours,
President.
Secretary treasurer.
I have another resolution from the North Pine Farmers' Institute, which is in the same area, as follows:
Whereas the immediate and pressing need of the western portion of the Peace River country is railway transportation facilities and more especially that vast section of newly settled country lying north of the Peace river and extending west from Hines Creek, the logical and ultimate need of the whole Peace country being a Pacific coast outlet directly west to tidewater,
And whereas the proposed Obed route is entirely inadequate to all but a small section in the southeast,
Therefore be it resolved that we, the members of the North Pine Farmers' Institute in general meeting assembled, unceasingly press for the immediate extension of the railway from Hines Creek westward to tap the Peace river block of British Columbia, to be extended eventually, as circumstances warrant, to the Pacific coast.
And now I wish to quote from a letter written by R. T. Elliott, and printed in the Grande Prairie Herald as Dawson Creek news in June of last year:
Referring again to the construction of the first section of the coast outlet railway, your correspondent received the following personal letter from Mr. R. T. Elliott. K.C., of Victoria re his recent reference to this problem, viz.:
Victoria, B.C.,
June, 3, 1934.
Many thanks for the Grande Prairie Herald of May 25. Delay in building to Finlay Forks is a crime. The trouble is to get truth into the

Peach River Outlet
east. People there cannot realize the comparatively small investment necessary to bring a new great west into buying power.
That is signed R. T. Elliott.
The editor goes on to comment on this letter in the following terms:
If that is the trouble-and we agree it may be, in part

then it is up to every public body interested in the early construction of a coast outlet to keep on bombarding the east with "the facts" regarding the economic soundness as well as the desirability of this road. That the argument no longer rests upon the agricultural traffic which would move in that direction but in addition there would be made available at once immense mineral areas which as Mr. Elliott says would bring "a new great west into buying power." We are convinced that of the many speeches made at Ottawa on the coast outlet resolutions, none made a deeper impression than that portion of John A. Fraser's address where he quoted "facts" regarding the Finlay Forks area. Various speakers following, expressed their surprise and deep interest in the "new angle" he had introduced to the government. Surely this offers some hint as to the spot where the political ice is the thinnest, so let us pile on the truth till the ice breaks in all directions.
That is -a comment on the address which I had given in which I attempted to lay before the house some facts in connection with the potentialities of Peace River. I am going to put on record some additional facts. I may not be able to get them all in on this occasion and I did not put them all on record when I spoke before. I have here a clipping from the Peace River Block News of August 31, 1934, in which the following statement appears:
The refusal of the railway company to extend their line from Hines Creek in to the north of the Peace River block may be excusable but it means that a large crop of grain which is being harvested in that fertile area will have to be hauled overland to Dawson Creek. . . . All supplies for the north and west have to be hauled by road from end of steel or the wholesale house at Dawson Creek and all grain and stock shipped out the same way. Surely the thousands of people depending on the roads for their very existence are deserving of some consideration.
That by the way is a criticism of the effort of the British Columbia government to keep the roads in condition. In other words, not only have they long distances to haul but the condition of the roads is hardly fit for travelling.
On many occasions the possibilities of the Peace River have been indicated and it is not necessary for me to put on the record any further facts in that regard, because they are now pretty well accepted. Last year I mentioned the mining possibilities in the area, and I would ask the house to bear in mind that the construction of the line from Hines Creek
to Hudson Hope would assist mining operations in that district. But I did not then include all mining operations, because I said little about coal. I outlined what was possible in connection with the precious metals as well as in copper, zinc and lead, but I scarcely touched on coal. Now I want to give a reliable estimate of the amount of coal in the Peace River area. This area lies at Hudson Hope and the particular area in which the coal lies-that is, the coal to which this estimate refers-is on the south side of Peace River. A strip seven miles long and one mile wide southwest of the canyon contains a definite estimated quantity of 85 million tons; that is the definite estimated tonnage. It has been looked over, surveyed and estimated by competent engineers and that is their estimate. Another strip seven miles long by one mile wide south of the first strip gives double this estimate, though this latter estimate is not definite. This gives you some idea of the quantity of coal available at Hudson Hope, and I suggest that there is opportunity for the distribution of that coal through the construction of the railway.
In addition to this we have possibilities of water power development in the canyon itself. Tributary to and along the river in various places we have large quantities of timber which could be made available for manufacturing purposes. The canyon itself is eighteen miles long and there is a drop in that eighteen miles of 270 feet, and the river itself is 200 feet wide. For that eighteen miles it goes between two walls of solid granite and is only 200 feet wide and, as I say, it drops in that distance 270 feet. If the whole flow could be utilized at one or more stages of development a minimum of 81,000 horse power could be developed, with a maximum of 245,000. That will give you some idea of the other potentialities of the district. All this is tributary to the Peace River and within the area which I am attempting to have served by further railway construction. I do not think I am in any way extravagant when I ask that the government give some attention to this matter at a very early date.
In order to show that things are moving in the district and that development is taking place, and to show that there is a certain amount of production, I want to quote from the Peace River Block News of January 25, 1935:
During the past year 356 carloads of settlers' effects were forwarded from Edmonton over the entire N.A.R. system, seventeen of these being unloaded at Dawson Creek (end of steel in B.C.), one at Pouce Coupe and one at Tupper.

In addition to these cars, many settlers trekked in with wagons, etc. There are thousands waiting for conditions to pick up, so that they can raise enough money from the sale of surplus stock and equipment to make the trip, to what one writer terms "The Glamorous Peace" and make a fresh start.
Although a wet fall affected the yields in the "Block" considerably it is estimated that between three-quarters of a million and one million bushels of grain will be shipped out during the 1934-35 crop year. To date about 300,000 bushels have already passed through the elevators.
As stated in a previous issue about $50,000 worth of cattle, sheep and hogs were shipped from the district. In addition eight carloads of horses have also been sent out, bringing in approximately $12,000 net to the sellers.
I could quote other statistics to show that a very substantial production is going on in that area from year to year, and that with the extension of railway service that production would greatly increase. My hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) indicated that the northern Alberta railways seemed to be economically operated. They are operated at about eighty per cent of the revenue which they earn, and while not paying all the costs of interest on the money invested in these roads they still do earn a substantial amount.
For my part I think it is reasonable to ask that a start be made on the construction of this road from the point of view of the employment it would provide not only in the area itself but from the standpoint of the assistance which it would give to business throughout the country as a whole. I submit that, both political parties having definitely and sincerely promised the people that this outlet would be built, the time is now opportune for a start to be made on it, continuing from year to year until an outlet is provided to the Pacific coast.

speechtext:
I would like to associate myself again with the mover of this resolution (Mr. Kennedy, Peace River) and with the hon, member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) who has so ably supported the suggestion. I am not in the position of those two hon. gentlemen of being wholly familiar by a long residence in those districts with all of the different points which might arise in this discussion. I cannot, like them, describe in detail the varied needs, the varied resources, the potential and actual wealth of that great area, but as one coming from a different part of the west, from central Alberta, I would like to indicate the feeling which exists among the inhabitants there toward their more northerly brethren. I would like also to place particular stress upon two points which seem to me to make the

immediate commencement of this project an urgent matter, and to point to the fact that this is indeed the logical time to make that commencement.
One aspect which is becoming of increasing importance and urgency is that which has relation to the great drought problem of other parts of Alberta and of the west generally, and to the fact that increasingly during the last years the Peace River country has been the mecca of those who have found themselves unable to continue in agriculture in the dried out areas. Thousands to my knowledge have set their eyes upon that district; thousands have already moved there and thousands now contemplate leaving the barren areas where they now reside and commencing a new Life in that newer country. I might point out, as has been indicated so well by previous speakers, that in the Peace River area you find the last great west, the last great fertile district which is at present but scantily served by transportation facilities. You find in it the last great area of agricultural land which is well supplied by nature with moisture, where the soil is of a fertile character and where real opportunity is afforded not only for the production of new wealth but for something which 1 think is of still greater importance-the creation of permanent homes. The eyes of people from the less fortunate areas have been directed there. Many have gone and they have found that the greatest handicap which they must overcome is, first, their distance from the railroad, a distance which must be experienced to be appreciated, for one who has not lived under such conditions cannot possibly realize what it means to be attempting to raise farm or any other products fifty, sixty or a hundred miles from the nearest railroad. I must confess that my recollection of that situation is not of recent years, but I have a very vivid recollection as a young man of central Alberta, for I had the dubious pleasure of going there when no railways had been built north of Calgary and when we were depending for our supplies upon a railway a hundred miles away and for our mail upon an occasional stage coach. I think I can still in memory appreciate the situation of settlers in the Peace River area.
Then too, they are facing another handicap: the excessive cost of shipping their products to the markets. It is true that arrangements have -been made, which under all the circumstances are perhaps somewhat fair, so that the entire additional cost of shipping their stuff back the hundreds of miles to Edmonton and then again westward to the

Peace River Outlet
coast is not borne wholly by the settlers; but the additional cost is very heavy; I think it averages perhaps five to five and a half cents a bushel on wheat and when you subtract from the prices other farmers have been receiving during the latter years that additional four and a half, five or five and a half cents a bushel which those settlers must pay, you will see that additional subtraction from the low price of their product may mean the difference between success and failure. Many are now rather deterred from entering that country because of fear of inability to settle within reasonable distance of a railway and because of the cost they must incur in shipping out their grain.
There is another aspect which to my mind makes the situation exceedingly urgent. Those of us who remember, as many of us do, the real opening up and the large settlement of western Canada in the beginning of this century will recall that development rested mainly upon two certain factors. The first was the free lands, the homesteads that were offered and the opportunity afforded to men to establish themselves in agriculture at relatively little cost. Most of them however were without funds and the second factor was the one which assisted them in making their settlement; that is, that the beginning of the century was marked not only by the opening up of a great west but by a tremendous program of railway construction. Thousands and tens of thousands of those settlers were able to finance themselves and to tide over their first hard years by working on the railways, by assisting in constructing the right of way. That is a matter which should be before the members of the government at the present time. To-day and during the past months and years in the Peace River hundreds of settlers have gone there, forced perhaps from their own farms by despair and failure, starting again under more favourable auspices, but without funds and compelled to rely upon relief for subsistence during those hard years. I suggest that under those circumstances it would be the part of wisdom were a program of construction moderate in cost and degree to be carried on which not only would -bring to the people of that country the transportation facilities to which I among many believe they are entitled, but would provide work for those who are making a fresh start and enable them to avoid being placed on public relief, thus maintaining their own morale, their self-respect and enabling them to pay back in the form of useful work and construction which would be of value during the coming years, the money which was paid to them.
In consideration of those two points and in consideration of the development which is only just commencing, of the opportunities afforded and of the drought problem which requires relief, I believe this is an opportune time to make at least a commencement upon that work to which every political body in Canada is committed, a work which every economist has declared sound, in order to provide for that last great railwayless area in the west the transportation facilities which will make it in the future a prosperous country, a country of homes and wealth producer for this dominion.

This government operates under the Department of National Defence unemployment camps. I am told that in those camps there are about 8,000 homeless men getting 20 cents a day together with indifferent board and clothing, for which they are expected to do some work. To my mind that is a disgrace to the people of Canada, and an insult to the intelligence of the men in those camps. I have visited some; I have three or four of them in my riding. After the last session I wrote the minister suggesting that instead of carrying on that disgraceful plan those men be paid a minimum wage for a short working day and in cooperation with the British Columbia government put to work to finish the Pacific Great Eastern from Burrard inlet to Prince George. both railways, in the heyday of prosperity, went too deeply into the construction of branch lines throughout the west.
I shall not take very long, but if I may I should like to review the whole question very briefly. My hon. friend from Peace River and the hon. member for Cariboo felt that they had dealt with this question so often that they merely brought forward new material, and I think both hon. gentlemen presented splendid arguments. They did not review the situation, however, and in a few words I should like to mention the different propositions. There have been proposals in regard to four outlets from the Peace River district, the Aggie-Obed route, which would link up with the Canadian National on the east side of the territory; the Monkman pass route, the Peace pass route and the Pine pass route. Just before the crash of 1929 the two railways were leaning rather strongly towards the Peace pass outlet, which would connect up the Peace River territory with the Pacific Great Eastern railway, which was mentioned by my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat. But when the crash came the two railways, headed at that time by Mr. E. W. Beatty and the late Sir Henry Thornton, took the attitude, which they have maintained consistently since, that they could not afford to go into any expansion of this kind. They took the position that if branch lines or outlets were to be constructed from the Peace River territory the country would have to do it alone, with no assistance of any kind from the railways except perhaps in connection with operation. They took the attitude that at least ten times the present traffic would be necessary to make the outlet by the Peace pass pay.
There have been four investigations into this question. I should like to refer to the last one, the investigation of 1932. I have in my hand Hansard of last year, from which I should like to quote the report in connection with that investigation, because it puts the whole situation in a concise form. That commission was made up of Mr. Gzowski of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Fair-bairn of the Canadian Pacific Railway and Mr. Crysdale, who was recommended by the province of British Columbia. I Should like to read three paragraphs from their conclusions:
In view of the above, our conclusions are:
1.	No western outlet is justified for the present, as the existing railway furnishes the most economical route. It will take many times the present traffic to justify another railway-outlet.
2.	The Obed route -

Peace River Outlet

To which I have just referred.
[DOT]-for a western outlet is the most favourable from a railway economic standpoint, considering the present phase of the railway situation.
While it is not mentioned it must be admitted by those who understand the territory that the Aggie-Obed route, to which I have referred, would mean a considerable amount of back haul.
3. We recommend that the matter of a final route be decided when the question is a practical one, believing that by the time the volume of traffic has reached a point where a western outlet is justified, general and possible local conditions may have materially changed. When the decision is imperative, the whole situation should be reviewed, in order to appraise all the contributing factors, including the potential traffic which may accrue from the lines beyond the definite areas included in this report.
That is a summing up of their report. It .nay be added, as I pointed out last year, that Dot only did Mr. Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton agree with this report, but Mr. Brownlee, then Premier of Alberta, appeared before the royal commission and took very much the same attitude. As a matter of fact Mr. Brownlee went so far as to say that in his opinion, and in the opinion of the government of Alberta, it was not so much an outlet from the Peace River district that was required as it was more branch lines. That was his conclusion, after giving the matter a good deal of study, and I must confess that I never saw Mr. Brownlee here in Ottawa at any of the interprovincial conferences without being impressed with the fact that he was one of the sanest and ablest of the western men attending those conferences.
I merely add this word, that the total program is still out of the question; I am quite frank about that. The people of Canada simply have not sufficient money at the present time to embark on a program embracing anything like the complete Peace River project, which would cost anywhere from $13,000,000 to $75,000,000 or $80,000,000, according to the number of branch lines required. Speaking personally, however, because the matter has not been discussed at any length, I must say that I am impressed with the proposal of the hon. member for Cariboo, in association with the hon. member for Peace River, that something should be done looking to the ultimate construction of a westerly outlet from the Peace River area. I may say quite sincerely that so far as I am concerned I shall endeavour to have this matter given fair and reasonable consideration.
It must be pointed out, as well, that since this section became settled the rates have been brought down very materially. For example,
(Mr. Manion.]
in 1921 the rate on grain from Grande Prairie to Fort William was 63J cents per hundred pounds. In 1925 the rate was reduced to 35i cents, not much more than half the former rate, and that is the rate in effect to-day. In 1921 the rate on grain from Grande Prairie to Vancouver was 58 J cents; it is now 28 cents, or less than half the previous rate. While some aid has been afforded in that way, it does not, of course, assist the settler who is 50 or 100 miles from railway service of any kind; I am quite free to admit that. It is true that world conditions are improving, I think with reasonable rapidity, and as the hon. member for Peace River has pointed out conditions in Canada have been improving as well. Last year the two railways combined, namely the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways, took in of gross revenue about $27,000,000 more than they did in the previous year. I believe the hon. members for Peace River and Cariboo, and other hon. members who may be interested to a lesser degree, may feel that there is more hope at the present time of something being done than there has been for some years. At the same time we must remember that even last year, with increased traffic, the Canadian Pacific Railway earned only sufficient to pay its bonded indebtedness, and the Canadian National Railway is still about a million dollars per week short of paying the interest charges on its bonded indebtedness.
I am going to take the liberty again-and I hope the hon. member will accept my suggestion-of moving the same amendment I moved last year. I assure him most sincerely that I do not move the amendment with any desire of stalling his proposal, but I do it entirely from the standpoint of honesty. It is possible that the house could accept the hon. member's motion just as it stands, but it seems to me that with the addition of the words I suggested last year, namely "when circumstances permit" the expression of the house could be made a little more honest. Otherwise, an acceptance of the motion as it now stands would be merely a pious hope and would perhaps give a greater amount of encouragement than I, in my innate honesty, desire to give. As amended the resolution would read:
That in the opinion of this house the Peace River country should be connected by a direct railway outlet to the Pacific coast, when circumstances permit.
In moving the amendment I have not in mind any desire to delay the purpose the hon. member has in mind, but it is moved so as to be quite frank with the people in that section of the country, with the hon. member and

Cooperative Commonwealth
hon. members who supported him. I would add merely this that at least I feel quite impressed with the idea that something might well be begun at the present time not only to assist the people of the Peace River section ana to give them hope for the future, but as a method of assisting in unemployment relief. I assure the hon. member and other hon. members that I shall endeavour to bring about something in the shape of assistance along that line.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, since the capitalist system is failing to function in the interests of the great majority of the people of Canada, it should be superseded by a cooperative commonwealth in which the profit motive would be subordinated to that of public service and ruthless competition replaced by collective ownership under democratic control.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, a few days ago
when the trade agreements were under discussion the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn) commented on the fact that I had protested against the time being spent on a discussion of matters which had been dealt with several years ago, and that the suggested motion was simply one of confidence in tho government. He very ingeniously suggested that I should be the last person to protest because the resolution standing in my name was in effect a vote of confidence in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. In one respect he is correct, but he failed to catch my point, namely, that in the resolution then being discussed we were asked to endorse a decision which had been made three years ago. In this resolution we are asked to endorse certain principles which we trust will be accepted in years to come.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext: You did the same thing two years ago.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext:
Three years ago my proposal along these lines seemed to some rather academic. However two years ago when I introduced a similar resolution I was in a position to call attention to the formation of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federa-ation. Last year matters had advanced to a stage where we were able to present a carefully considered program. After the past year and a half we are in a position to report still further advances, because in the three provincial elections, namely in British Columbia. Saskatchewan and Ontario, some 300,000 votes were polled for the candidates of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I interpret that fact to mean that 300,000 people have endorsed the resolution I now have the honour to move. In the provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is now the official opposition. Recently in the cities of Winnipeg, St. Boniface, Windsor and Toronto men identified with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have been elected mayors. For these reasons I submit the matter before us is no longer academic.
Before we may bring forward a suggestion of a new social order it is necessary to convince the general public of the bankruptcy of the old order. To-day I have very great pleasure in calling as my chief witness no other than the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself. I regret that at the moment he is not in his seat, but I believe we owe him a debt of gratitude for his radio speeches in that for the first time a Prime Minister of Canada has frankly recognized that the present system is no longer sacrosanct and has himself taken the lead in condemning that system. The Prime Minister expressly suggests that the capitalist system should be judged on its merits. In my view that is an excellent statement. In his first radio speech he said, "The economic system will be examined without prejudice," and further, "If it has failed we must change it." That has given me courage to suggest in what ways it should be changed.
I would call attention to the fact that in their comments newspapers seem to have had the idea that we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation want to abolish capital. According to the economist capital is simply that wealth which is used to produce new wealth. Our capital consists of our mines, our factories, our railways and so on. No one wants to abolish capital, but what we do suggest is the abolition of the capitalist system, namely the system under which wealth is largely concentrated in the hands of a few. In its modern form at least, that system is of comparatively recent origin. It has grown up in the last one hundred and fifty years, since the introduction of machines into Great Britain, with the resulting organization of industry, commerce and finance. We desire, then, to abolish a system whereby the control of those means of production is so largely centred in the hands of a few.
Cooperative Commonwealth

The Prime Minister further has recognized that the capitalist system did serve a useful function. I quite agree with him in that. He says:
The old system served you well, but it ended in a nuisance. Is that so or not. It ended in
a condition under which there has been universal depression and unemployment and poverty in the midst of plenty.
If that is true, and I quite agree with the Prime Minister, then it is high time that we began to ask ourselves whether we cannot discover some system which will lead us out of our difficulties.
The Prime Minister also very thoughtfully discussed the question that bothers a good many, and that is: If the system worked well in the past, why should it not continue to work? I quote the Prime Minister again:
Possibly some of you will maintain that because the system has served us well in the past there is a presumption in favour of its continuing to do so in the future, but clearly there is no proof that it will do so. Indeed present conditions are surely proof that it will not.
And he goes on to say it should be reformed. Now I would go further than the Prime Minister went in this regard. I believe that the present system cannot work much longer. It worked in England a hundred years ago because her surplus products were exported to other countries. At first it was merefy commodities that were exported, but later on we find the export of capital goods, and then when the system was set up in other countries there came about that extreme rivalry that led to a great many international complications and that finally I believe was the basic cause of the world war. Those who had been our customers became our competitors, and we have now reached the stage when nearly all the more forward nations have adopted the capitalist system. Japan is the last great nation to adopt it, and to-day we know that owing to their efficiency and their lower standards of living, and perhaps to the depreciation of their currency and other financial factors, the Japanese are able to outbid some of the older capitalist countries in the markets of the world.
Now we face the fact that nearly all countries are attempting to get these outside markets. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is elementary that goods must be sold either at home or abroad. Until recently we have had an expanding foreign market, but to-day that market has ceased to expand and in fact it is beginning to contract for every country. No nation can hope to have the same opportunities that it had before.
tMt. Woods worth.]
What about our home market? Here is where we get into difficulties because under this capitalist system the people have not the consuming power to buy back what is produced; that is the real difficulty to-day. The government faces somewhat the same difficulty when they find it next to impossible to pay the interest on their bonded indebtedness and at the same time to extend social services. If they could extend social services, undoubtedly that would help to lift the depression, but they cannot do that and at the same time pay the interest on their bonded indebtedness. Industry is in much the same position. If it were possible for employers of labour in Canada to double their payrolls in every direction it might be possible to get things moving and to recover prosperity again, but I venture to say there are very few employers to-day who are in a position to increase their payrolls and at the same time meet their interest charges and overhead expenses. So that governments and the industrial world alike are prohibited from doing the very thing and the only thing that would save the situation. There is the anomaly that faces the world.
I have said before, and I repeat it, that years ago when I was trying to read some social economics I could not understand the phrase that was often used, "the inherent contradictions of capitalism," but I think we have reached the period when the inherent contradictions are beginning to manifest themselves. I submit that what worked a hundred years ago when only one nation had adopted the system is not working to-day when almost all the leading nations of the world have adopted this system. I could not get a better witness than the Prime Minister to testify to the evils which have developed under capitalism. I quote him:
Many faults and injustices in the capitalist system . . . child labour, sweat shops, slave wages, crushingly long hours, inequality of benefits, low prices to the primary producers, high prices to the ultimate consumer.
The Prime Minister must surely have been reading the evidence given before the price spreads committee because that is a very fair 'summary of the evils revealed in the evidence there. The Prime Minister goes on:
The selling price .... sometimes influenced by unconscionable monopolistic purchasers or by certain types of middlemen and distributors, some of whose activities would properly include them within the class of economic parasites.
I always like the Prime Minister's phrases. "Economic parasites" is a good phrase, and I have no doubt it will be re-echoed on a great

many soap boxes across the country. In fact, I rather think the Prime Minister caught it from some soap box orator.

speechtext:
I know it might be possible for the federal government to transfer this matter to the provinces, to have an unemployment insurance scheme to which certain classes would be asked to contribute and from which certain classes would receive benefits. That is all very well, but it does not touch the half million people now out of work, who together with their dependents number over a million. What does the Prime Minister propose to do with them? So far there is no answer, and I think we have to admit that since the right hon. gentleman is the Prime Minister of the country, since be earlier recognized that unemployment was a national problem, he must either abolish the dole or, if we are to use discipline, we insist that we abolish the system.
I am glad to say that the Prime Minister, for the first time as far as I am aware, has also frankly recognized that the trouble does not lie in the weaknesses of individuals. A great many people say that if a man is out of work it is his own fault. Or that if a man is overcharging or exploiting the public you have to deal with him; because he has not the love of God in his heart he should be curbed in some way. I perceive that these gibes are being directed not against me, but against the Prime Minister.
Only last Saturday we had a meeting of the council of our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and I was very glad to have that council draw up a statement of our position in view of the Prime Minister's so-called reform legislation. This was not a preelection manifesto, as the papers had it. I should like to read a few paragraphs-it was in some of the papers this morning:
In the opinion of the National Council of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation the program of the federal government is entirely inadequate to meet the situation.
Reform or reconstruction; that is the issue.
That capitalism has broken down even the old parties now agree. Debt, unemployment, insecurity, the hopeless position of youth, are signs of an economic system in decay. Their persistence and the failure of reform measures in all countries confirm the repeated declarations of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in respect to the economic problem.
The old parties tell us that the system can be patched up by "reforms." But if reforms have not solved the problem in other countries how can the same reform solve it in Canada?
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes that capitalism can be neither reformed nor restored: Profit for the few and prosperity for the masses are incompatible. The only permanent solution of our problems is to get rid of capitalism and replace it by a new social order, the cooperative commonwealth.
Effective reconstruction must begin where human suffering is greatest. We therefore propose the following as the first steps towards the cooperative commonwealth:
(1)	Finance:
Socialization of all financial institutions so as to secure control of prices and production and to finance socially useful public works and services by national credit.
(2)	Agriculture:
(a)	Adequate minimum income for the farmer as a first charge on his production.
(b)	Statutory reduction of the farmer's debts, with prevention of forclosure and eviction.
(c)	Planned extension of markets for farm products.
(d)	Bringing the price level of what the farmer sells into line with the price level of what he buys.
(e)	Encouragement of producers' and consumers' cooperatives.
(f)	Socialization of packing and other processing plants.
(3)	Labour and Social Services:
(a)	An immediate large-scale program of socially useful public works, including housing financed by public credit.
(b)	A national minimum wage to give every family a standard of living commensurate with the nation's capacity to produce wealth.
(c)	Protection and encouragement of trade unions and workers' organizations, and an
effective voice for the workers in the management of industry.
(d)	National non-contributory social insurance with adequate benefits against unemployment, sickness, accident, old age and death.
(e)	Socialized health services.
(f)	The six hour day and five day week, to be increased or decreased according to social need.
(g)	Abolition of relief camps.
The carrying through of even these proposals will, of course, involve extensive socialization of industry and social planning, as outlined in the Regina manifesto of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation.

I should like to refer to a statement issued by the North American Life Association Company as the result of an investigation conducted by them. They take one hundred men at twenty-five years of age, and show that at the end of forty years, when most of these men have reached the end of their earning ability, sixty-one will be living and thirty-

nine will have died. Of the sixty-one still living, fifty-two or more than fifty per cent of the original number, will be living on charity or will be dependent upon the assistance of friends and relatives, leaving only nine who will be independent. Of the nine, five will be working for a living, while four will have earned and set aside enough for their old age. This would seem to indicate that under present conditions it is very difficult for the average man to lay aside sufficient during his working years to take care of his old age, which would seem to show that something is wrong with the system under which we have been operating up to the present time. This depression has caused great distress throughout the country, and I should like to read the solution suggested by the ex-kaiser with regard to this point:
1.	Unemployment cannot be cured by material means alone, for it is " spiritual distress."
2.	While it is true that the machine threatens our entire economic life, yet the mind of man, which created the machine, will also "find ways and means of effectively meeting the excesses of technics."
3.	One effective way of meeting unemployment is that of taking industrial workers out of the big cities and away from the machine-dominated factory, and "putting them to work at building streets and canals, or cultivating waste land, or colonizing them" as small farmei's.

In his seclusion in Holland the ex-kaiser has been able to view what has been going on in the rest of the world.
The proposition advanced by my hon. friend is simply a socialistic program. Socialism has not been a success in the world. I should like to quote from a very pertinent article written by a Toronto man named Frederic Davidson. I do not know who he is, but his remarks go right to the point. He says:
Socialism would socialize initiative-and slay it; would submerge the gifted who alone bring forth all that makes life worth living here below. Socialism takes from those who have, by reason of their initiative and self reliance, and gives to those who have not, who never could have otherwise, without these qualities. Socialism thinks it can get nothing without taking what belongs to others. And in this it sees clearly, for socialism is sterile, non-productive.
Socialism never has produced anything in the world and never will, because it takes the people in the mass and not by the individual. The individual who has initiative.

Cooperative Commonwealth
courage and ability has always produced what has made the world better. The London Morning Post recently contained a very interesting article, from which I should like to read
a few sentences:
"The moral and intellectual wealth of a nation," says Galton, "largely consists in the multifarious variety of the gifts of the men who compose it, and it would be the very reverse of improvement to make all its members assimilate to a common type. . . . "Civilizations," says Gustave Le Bon, "have been created and directed, not by crowds, but by a small intellecual aristocracy. . . . Nor can education make men equal, since it confirms the inferior mind in its inferiority while strengthening the superior mind in its superiority.
Evolution, then, does not equalize; it differentiates, and not only in individuals, but in classes. Man is said to have emerged from a primitive communism, in which all enjoyed the cold and precarious equality of the cave-level; but he has been sorted out in the course of ages into classes and vocations, every one the complement of the others, and now lives in an ordered society, highly complex and infinitely differentiated. By an atavistic impulse the socialist would obliterate all class differences and reduce mankind to its original state.
In other words socialism would reduce all classes to a common level, and all classes would be controlled by the state. Eventually there would be only two classes, the governors and the governed, and in a few generations we would be back where we were many centuries ago. Then the old fight for freedom and liberty would have to be fought all over again. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says we have no liberty of speech in Canada to-day. I say we have in Canada to-day the greatest liberty of speech the world has had at any time. At the present time a man can say almost anything he likes so long as he does not advocate violence against the state. If Mr. Tim Buck comes to Ottawa he will have the privilege of addressing any number of people he can get to listen to him, if he will simply keep within the law.
Capitalism has been blamed for all the ills of life. The hon. member moving the resolution said that capitalism has outlived its usefulness, and that it must be done away with. I want to say that capitalism has been a great success, and in essence it is sound and will prevail. The capitalist is the only fly in the ointment. He is the man who has caused all the distress of the world, and he must be eliminated-not the capitalist system, but the capitalist himself. Capitalism has produced a superabundance of all the necessities and luxuries of life, and at the same time it has eliminated the sweat from the brow
of man. It has made this system the greatest and most wonderful in the world's history. To talk of scrapping a system which has given such service is plain insanity. I say that to the hon. member, and any man who talks about scrapping the capitalistic system must have a loose cell in his brain and ought to have a surgical operation to cement it into place.
