member undertake to do the job?
Mr. ANDERSON (Halton); Probably in the case of the hon. member it would be a little dangerous. Any system which can produce such overabundance with so little labour can and will distribute its benefits to all classes of humanity, if it is given time to adjust itself to our changing needs.
I emphasize again, as I did two years ago, that the change must come gradually and imperceptibly. Impatience would create an upheaval which would destroy the system and the people themselves. We are moving rapidly enough towards a socialistic state. During the last few years we have been going in that direction very rapidly, and if we continue to follow that course we will have a socialistic system unless we bolster up the capitalistic system. I am not advocating a policy of laissez-faire, but I am supporting the policy enunciated by the Prime Minister in the speech from the throne. I would recommend eliminating the defects in the capitalistic system and bringing it up to date. The utopia envisioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre cannot function to-day; it cannot function until the human heart has been purged of greed and selfishness. That has been the cause of the downfall of the capitalistic system.
I have but a few more remarks to make, because I realize my voice is not in good condition to-day. Two years ago I advocated that the government would be wise to set up a system whereby certain of the unemployed men eligible for such work could return to small acreages of land. The idea was to take many of these men out of the towns and put them on small acreages, give them some assistance in the building of their houses, and instructions as to how to work their property. As a result they would have a stake in the country, and I believe in a few years they would be in a position to pay back what they had borrowed from the government. Some who are now discontented would be satisfied; they would have something to do, and would not be standing about on street corners and criticizing other people.
Cooperative Commonwealth

A few days ago I read in the Ottawa Journal an article written by a man from Gatineau, Quebec, who signs himself "J.J.F." Although not formerly a farmer his statement indicates he would like to get back to the land. These are his words:
To one who, like myself, looks over his shoulder at the forty-years-old dead line, the question obtrudes itself "Whither goest thou?" The answer always is: "I do not know." And there are many who must make the same unsatisfactory reply.
There could, however, be a different one. There is a solution for such as I. Merely the agency to give it effect is lacking. It is a modified "baek-to-the-land" movement. Not back to the farm-I have never done farming on a large scale-but back to the land nevertheless: To the large garden and the raising of fowl, etc. These things I have done, and could do again. It is no royal road to riches but it is a highway to a living, to peace of mind, to self respect and to the lost luxury of work. It would put back the "dead line" another twenty years.
There must be, I am sure, many suitable locations for such an enterprise, which are now either temporarily vacant or abandoned. The only immediate needs are two to five acres of land, a house that can be made habitable and water. Given such a location free for one year, I would guarantee to pay rent thereafter and eventually to buy. There are many others, I feel certain, who would take advantage of such an opportunity.
That is one way to employ the unemployed. From the Chicago Daily News I have extracted the following to indicate the cost of employing the unemployed in public works undertakings:
There is no costlier form of relief than public works. Take one point of the new program, the elimination of grade crossings. The New York Times has made a study of the elimination last year of a grade crossing at Great Neck, New York, half by the state, half by the Long Island Railroad. The job gave direct employment to 185 men for eleven months at an average cost per man of $3,500. Direct relief for each man would have cost $432. To employ these men, in this case, cost eight times as much as direct relief would have cost.
That is a most interesting commentary on the expensive proposition of giving employment to unemployed through a program of public works.
In the reconstruction program proposed I would -ask the government not to forget the largest class in the dominion, namely the middle class. If we are to judge by the present attempts being made towards reconstruction it is obvious the middle class will get the worst of it. They do not get any benefits from government relief. They are too wealthy to obtain relief from the government, but they are not wealthy enough to obtain the services given to labour, services which the wealthy can quite easily pay for.

When they reach old age these people are dependent upon the money they have invested in bonds, stocks and securities of different kinds. The tendency to-day is to reduce the interest rates on -those bonds or stocks. In a few years these people, who are now selfsustaining and would be in a position to maintain themselves in their old age, will be on the list of unemployed and will have to receive relief. I should like to ask the government, municipal authorities and industrial concerns to -have consideration for and help to keep solvent that class which has paid by far the greatest amount in taxes.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in support of the resolution now before the house, I may say that I shall not take very much time to answer the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson) who spoke just before the dinner recess. I can assure him that the party to which I belong has changed neither its program nor its name, although he may think so. As a matter of fact what he really thought was a change on our part was that he was hearing advocated in other quarters some of the policies we have been advocating for years, and becoming more familiar with them he does not now think them so wild and terrible as they appeared to him two years ago. The change really has been in himself and not in us.
The hon. gentleman made certain statements which he himself proceeded to answer. He said that socialism had never been a success anywhere. Then he told us that we were proceeding as rapidly as possible towards socialism, which from his point of view cannot be a desirable thing. Then he told us that capitalism was an unqualified success, and from statistics went on to prove that about eighty per cent of the people under the capitalist system died in poverty, leaving no property, not even enough to bury them. With that I agree.
I should like to answer the question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) as to who is going to pay for all these social improvements we are suggesting. Who is going to pay for all these improvements in human society? As a matter of fact, I think it is fairly easy to tell him who is going to pay for them. Wealth can be and is produced only by applying human labour to natural resources. Then those who are going

Cooperative Commonwealth
to pay for everything are those who apply that labour. When we look around us and see the wealth on every hand-our great cities, our farms, our great industries', our railways-that is the wealth of the world, and that has been created by human labour. The reason we are in the depression we are in to-day, Mr. Speaker, is because labour did not get enough for producing that wealth, and that is the answer to my hon. friend's question as to who is going to pay.
The thought in this resolution is the most important question before the people of the civilized world to-day. It is the topic of conversation wherever a few people are gathered together. That is, can the present capitalist system be reformed, or what are we going to put in its place? These are the questions that are uppermost in the minds of thinking people to-day, and anyone who does not consider that question important is dead from the chin up.
Two years ago when a similar resolution was moved in this house there was a great deal of opposition to it, of course, and no doubt there are a great many people to-day who will not accept the thought embodied in the resolution. However, regardless of the reception which the resolution may receive, I am quite satisfied that the ideas which we are putting forward are making progress and are meeting with a more and more favourable reception every day.
I have said that almost all thinking people the world over who are giving any thought to the questions of the day are inquiring and thinking about these changes that must come about. I recollect that last session the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) touched on this subject in his speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At page 612 of Hansard of 1934 he said in part:
If I may take just a few more minutes I should like to conclude with a few observations upon a subject which I regard as of even greater importance.
That was of even greater importance than the question he had just been discussing. He went on:
I believe that by legislation of some sort, by planning or by some adjustment, there should be brought about in this country a condition whereby the spread between the return to labour and the return to capital should not be so great. 1 have made that statement before in this house. I do not know whether it is the enunciation of a socialist doctrine, but I believe that if the man who produces, who labours on the farm, in the factory-and perhaps I am thinking more particularly of the factory-in the mine or elsewhere does not
receive enough money in return to enable him to buy back that which he produces, you are bound to have depression.
That is very clear, and as I said a moment ago, the reason we have this depression to-day is that those who have produced the wealth of the world have not received sufficient for producing it to enable them to consume or use it. The hon. member for North Waterloo went on:
I am not going to say just how that is going to be brought about. My friends in the corner say that it can be done only by entirely scrapping the present system. I am not ready to go so far as that; I do not believe my hon. friends in the corner of the house are ready to take hold of matters and bring all these things about. If we did anything of that kind I fear we might end in chaos, a condition which would be worse than what we have to-day.
Of course, whether it would be better or worse would depend altogether upon the person who is speaking. I know a great many people in this dominion who think that their condition at the present time could not be any worse than it is now. I am doubtful if the hon. member for North Waterloo realizes what we mean when we say that this system must be scrapped or abolished. I hope he has not in his mind the idea that we wish to destroy the capital or industrial equipment that we now have. That is not what we mean at all, and no sensible person who gave the matter a moment's thought would suggest that we were thinking of anything of that kind. Capital is not so much a material thing as it is a social relabionshp, and it is that social relationship and the purpose for which we now use capital that will have to be abolished or scrapped-whichever word you prefer-and not the equipment itself. When we have changed the purpose of production, that is, when we begin to produce things to meet the needs of the community and not for the purpose of making profits for the owners of the machinery of production, then we have abolished capitalism; but we have not abolished the equipment and the instruments of production, which is altogether a different thing.
I should like to quote an authority who has been quoted in this house on previous occasions, if the hon. member for Temiscouata will bear with me in this. Sir Arthur Salter, who has also been on the air recently, makes this statement:
We cannot restore the old competitive system. We must recognize that there must be increasing socialization and increasing control of such activities as are not completely socialized.
Two years ago Sir Arthur Salter would not have gone so far as that, but he has been
Cooperative Commonwealth

thinking. He has been observing the development of economic conditions, and he has come to the conclusion that there is no solution for our problems except more and more socialization, more control of the means of production and distribution.
The resolution now before the house is in two parts. The first contains a statement of fact, that the capitalist system is failing to function in the interest of the great majority of the people of Canada. There is not the slightest doubt about that. The second part of the resolution recommends that since the present system is failing to function it should be replaced by a system that will function. Although the resolution does not say so explicitly, the implication is there that the system is failing to function because it is based on the profit motive. Consequently the resolution asks that the present system be superseded by a system from which the profit motive will be eliminated, so that instead of competing for rewards we should cooperate for social benefit.
What should be the objective of any rational system of production-any economic system? The rational objective of any economic system should be the supplying of the social needs of the people as fully and on as equitable a basis as possible. Measured by these two reasonable and attainable ideals, our present system, everyone must agree, has broken down and the opponents of the resolution must admit the failure of the system or else in some logical way justify the glaring paradox of our time, poverty in the midst of plenty. Those who disagree with the resolution virtually maintain that property rights are more important than human rights; that on the one side are the few with property and on the other side the many with their needs, and that they are going to stand with the few and with property. There is no middle course whereby each should have consideration. If we follow profit then we must leave the road that leads to social service, and vice versa. I have here a copy of a pamphlet which I believe each of the members has received. It is a report of the findings of a commission which was appointed by the United Church of Canada in 1932. After considerable study the commission embodied their findings in this report, the title of which is Christianizing the Social Order, and the report is signed by Sir Robert Falconer and Doctor W. T. Brown of Victoria College, Toronto. In a paragraph dealing with the defects of modern industry they say:
Despite the enormous gains made possible by the employment of modern science in the service of human needs, we are confronted with a new fact-dire want in the midst of plenty. 
Production is deliberately restricted and produce is destroyed, not because it is not needed, but because that procedure promises higher prices. Human energy is often diverted from the production of the essential needs of life to socially undesirable or useless ends. Both in towns and rural areas people are compelled to li''e, in dwellings which lack the ordinary conveniences of modern housing, or are so overcrowded as to make decency and health almost impossible; yet the material for building and the energy of builders are available in abundance.
I have read from this report because, on looking over the Parliamentary Guide, I find that a great many of the members of the house are members of the United Church of Canada, and I would ask them to take this report and study it closely. If they do so I am sure they will find that it goes a long way in the direction of what we have been advocating in this house for the last five years.
I wish to quote very briefly once more from the report of the commission, but before doing so I must touch on another point. We have sometimes been accused of stirring up class antagonisms and engendering class hate. To this we plead not guilty. These class antagonisms and this class strife were already in existence, created by the very conditions that create classes. If we have referred at any time to classes we have referred to them only as a physician might refer to a condition he found after examining his patient. We found certain conditions prevailing in human society; we found want and misery in the midst of abundance and consequently came to the conclusion that that want and that misery, side by side with abundance, could not possibly exist except in a society where there were classes. So that we are therefore no more responsible for what we have found than the physician is responsible for the disease he may find after he has diagnosed his patient's symptoms. In this regard I would quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). He has been quoted several times to-day, but I will put one or two more quotations on the record. In his radio address on January 4 he said:
Let us first examine income. To do so, I think it is helpful for the purpose of their discussion, to divide all recipients of income, from whatever sources, into two broad classes:' non-producers, and producers or workers. . , . The non-producer does not work for his income. It is his invested money which works.
He goes on to say:
# Now, we may divide the producer or worker into three basic classes: the rural and urban worker, the agriculturist, and what is sometimes colloquially called the white collar worker. ^ This latter class shares in common with their brethren in agriculture and industry,

Cooperative Commonwealth
the hardships of these times. Their problems are essentially the same and they stand in need of the same measure of relief from them.
All that is necessary to make that statement complete is to say, "Workers of the world, unite; you have nothing to lose but your chains. You have a world to gain."
To quote once more from the pamphlet to which I have already referred, Christianizing the Social Order:
The strife between classes and groups growing out of the social stratification based on income, and the economic struggle for a larger share of the product of industry, is a factor of increasing significance both in national and international life. The struggle enters the international field when national groups of producers or financiers seek privileged access to raw materials or markets. This economic nationalism has now become more perilous than at any other time, for those who seek privilege within the nation tend to influence governments and to evade control; and then in their exploitation of new fields they veil their private interests in the garments of national honour and glory. When they succeed in this the economic conflict passes over into international war.
The division of the country into classes, based on ownership or income, or the access to the means of life, leads therefore to strife. Not only does it create strife within the nation; it leads to strife outside it as well, and it leads, as the report says, to international war.
I will give a further example of this class division by referring to the United States. In the United States in 1933 was commenced a program which is sometimes called the Roosevelt experiment. All of us remember the extent to which when the present president of the United States came into office on March of that year, the industrial collapse had gone in that country; the whole economic life of the nation was almost paralyzed and the capitalist class there had no idea what to do to get out of the mess in which they found themselves. Mr. Roosevelt began putting his program into effect and at the beginning there was no obstruction whatever; the capitalist class of the United States were so discredited that they did not dare to raise their voices. Mr. Roosevelt began to use the nation's credit to start the wheels of industry going, and improvement began to take place. But the moment that was accomplished the resistance from the owning class of the United States began. That resistance has continued until to-day so that the new deal is in a state of collapse. Let me assure the Prime Minister that if he goes ahead with a radical program that is worth while, that will improve the
conditions of the masses of the people of this country, he will receive the same obstruction and opposition from the owning class here as President Roosevelt has received from the owning class in the republic to the south of us.
A short while ago I read in a book a statement-I believe the mover of the resolution (Mr. Woodsworth) made the statement today-that profits for the owners of capital and prosperity for the masses were entirely incompatible. Of course that is one reason why the present economic system cannot be reformed or restored. May I put the situation in this way: the necessity of making profits precludes the possibility of solving our problems under the present system. That is so because the capitalistic system is based essentially on the law of supply and demand; in other words, the law of supply and demand of goods and services is the governor which regulates business activity. Society itself is not supposed to take thought as to how its needs are to be supplied; that is left to the desire for gain which is inherent in all of us. No wonder we are in the difficult position in which we find ourselves! The theory is- and I believe it is correct-that where there is a demand for a commodity or service, people who have capital to invest will invest it in the production of that commodity or service. When the supply exceeds the demand, prices will fall and then capital will desert that particular field of production and seek a field in which the demand exceeds the supply. But when prices fall for the reason mentioned, profits also decrease. Therefore it becomes clear that in order that these people may continue making profits, the demand must always exceed the supply; that is, in order that profits may be made, we must have scarcity. The moment we enter into an age of abundance, such an age as we are living in now, at that moment profits become impossible. Man's ingenuity, his inventive genius, along with the kindness of nature has ushered us into an age of abundance, an age in which there is no scarcity, and consequently unlimited profits such as were made in the past are quite impossible.

Mr. MaeINNIS:	Except by creating an
artificial scarcity. There is however a very definite limit to that. The development of capitalism has created such a large industrial organization that large numbers of workers are divorced from all contact with their means
Cooperative Commonwealth

of livelihood and consequently have to be taken care of out of the earnings of industry in some way or another.
Some of our opponents are opposed to our policy because they say it will interfere with private property. That may be true in a sense, but the freeing of the chattel slaves also interfered with private property; yet will anyone say that that was not a step in human progress? The situation in which we find ourselves to-day is that we have slavery of another kind-the ownership of the means of production in the hands of a few and the great mass of the people without access to those means of production except on the terms laid down by their owners. Consequently they are just as much slaves as were the chattel slaves; all the freedom they have is to work, if any is available, on the terms laid down by the owners of industry, or to starve.
Property is of two kinds; there is property in the means of production, corporate property, which cannot be said to-day to be private property in any true sense of the term. No one can put his hands on the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Bank of Montreal or any of those large institutions and say: That is my property. It is corporate property. That kind of property has value to the people who say they own it or are the shareholders in it, because the community uses it. The moment the community ceases to use any kind of corporate property, it ceases to have any value. The railway companies complain about the competition of motor bus and motor truck transportation. What are they complaining about? What they are complaining about is that the community, the people of Canada, are transferring their patronage from the railways to the motor buses and trucks and consequently are taking the value out of the Canadian Pacific and putting it into the other form of transportation. What I think is quite a logical conclusion to come to is that if the people of the nation, because of using an institution of any kind, give value to it, the nation or the community should own it and use it and appropriate the proceeds of it, whatever they may be.
I would have liked, had there been time, to mention other objections that are sometimes raised to socialism, or to a cooperative system, whichever terra one cares to use. One of the objections I have heard on many occasions to socialism, is that it would break up the home. At home yesterday morning I listened to a service broadcast from one of the United churches in Ottawa, and I heard the pastor

pray for the homeless single men in our unemployment camps. It is strange that under a system of society that was going to preserve the home we should have in a great rich country such as Canada a class that we call homeless single men, or homeless men of any kind. It means that these men's homes have been broken up, that they have been deprived of their homes. To break up the home is one thing that socialism will not have to do; capitalism has already done it. A little less than a year ago the child welfare committee of the League of Nations took up the matter of the condition of child an in poor homes. A report in the Vancouver Daily Province of April 18, 1934, says:
Alarm over the disastrous effects of the depression everywhere is strongly expressed in the draft report of the league's child welfare committee made public at its meeting.
Struck by the serious character of psychological effects produced by depression upon children, and of the strained and discouraged family atmosphere which is inevitable in homes suffering from unemployment.
The committee emphasizes the necessity of removing children from the pernicious atmosphere of their own home during the greater part of the day and sending them to nursery schools, recreation centres and reading rooms in order that they may enjoy quietness and freedom from care and irritation which are essential conditions to their development.
The committee recommends all governments to reexamine their legislation with a view to safeguarding better unity of the family, assuring the child's development and protecting his self respect.
We agree with that. But I think we also agree and maintain, at any rate I do, that while under certain circumstances and for a certain part of the day a child should be in school or kindergarten from an early age, yet the child who is deprived of the love and care that it should receive in a proper home is forced into society under a handicap that he will never overcome. Even if for no other reason than that, it is time we considered our social organization. These young men in our unemployment camps will carry all their lives the scars of their present circumstances, but we should at least begin to make provision for the children yet unborn, the future citizens of this country, that they may be able to build up a country of which they may be proud, although we cannot be proud of the present conditions. But we are hoping for something better. It is because of the conditions that we find about us, for which capitalism has no answer, that we ask this house to take into consideration the immediate changing over of our economic system in order that the machinery of production may be released from the restrictions placed upon it by the profit

Cooperative Commonwealth
motive, allowing us to use it to the utmost to provide people with food, clothing and shelter and give access to a full cultural life for every citizen of this dominion.

speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, I shall answer
the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). He said this afternoon that he had not read the fifty-five questions that the member for Temiscouata had put to him on February 9, 1933. I admit the bon. gentleman may not have read them all, but he has heard a few of them, because they were recited in an audible voice in this house when he was here. The hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) said, as reported at page 1950 of Hansard:
Would the hon. member permit me to inform him that his questions are so hot that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has left the chamber.
Mr. Heaps: In deference to the hon. gentleman who has left the chamber, I think my hon. friend from South Essex ought to have first found out why he left it.
Then the member for Temiscouta continued :
I do not discuss that viewpoint. I simply wish to put my questions on record in Hansard in order that everyone may take cognizance of them. My next question follows-
Sir, it is very easy to understand what has been said in plain language in this house. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre heard about half the questions I directed to him, and then instead of staying to the end he left the house, a thing that he very seldom does. I am sorry that he left the house when I was not through asking him questions in very polite language. Those questions were not based on quotations from Sir Arthur Salter or from the United church or from a book whose author has not been named before by his son-in-law. They were based on pure logic. Logic is something with which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is not familiar; that is the main trouble with him, he has no logic. He has not the faculty of analyzing facts. He knows certain facts, but he does not distinguish between the system and the individual. I admit that capitalists have often been wrong. Widows who have in the bank the proceeds of insurance on the life of a husband now deceased are legitimate capitalists. In a different class of capitalist is the man who took advantage of the fact that he had supported the present government to request the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to increase the tariff, insinuating that trade might be
increased thereby, who lied to the government in telling them that if the tariff was raised he would employ more men and pay them better wages. That is one fault I find with capitalism-no, not with capitalism, but with certain capitalists. We have sharks in this country, I admit that; but from that are we to conclude that everyone who has property of some kind is to hand it over to the control of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre and my hon. friend from Vancouver South? Would it be safe for them to entrust all their investments and property to those who, though men of good faith, know nothing about the business of this country? That is not a harsh statement; I will prove it.
If all the bills these two hon. gentlemen have presented to this house had been adopted, do you think the capitalist system would have disappeared from this country? What did they do in this house to alter the laws on our statute books, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) since 1921 and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) since 1930? What is their record with regard to legislation? It is nil. They cannot even boast about getting the house to change section 98 of the criminal code; it was done by the Liberal party. If our social order is so bad why did not my hon. friends come to this house and do something to change the order? What are they doing to-day? My hon. friend from Vancouver South has introduced a bill to change the elections act. What has he tried to change in the social order of this country? It is all humbug and deceit. Was that intentional or was it not? Perhaps it was unconscious; the hon. member is here to say. Those hon. gentlemen come here with the shoes of the actors in Roman theatres, one pair for comedy and another pair for tragedy.
I hear these hon. gentlemen speak about the troubles of the workingmen in this country. I have a right to speak about those social matters, because when I was on the other side of the house I was the first member to quote figures with regard to employment and low wages in the province of Quebec; my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre remembers that. My hon. friend from Vancouver South will not remember, because he was not in the house then. Before the labour members did anything with regard to working conditions in my native province I gave figures, which are on record in Hansard, showing how the workingmen of my province were paid in comparison with the workingmen in other provinces. I was a humble man, a lawyer, not a tram conductor, not a man

Cooperative Commonwealth

working on the wharves of Vancouver but a lawyer who meets people and tries to do his best for them. I was and am a humble man, but a man of sincerity and a man who knew where he was going. I worked for a long time with the officials of the Department of Labour, and from the bottom of my heart I thank Hon. Peter Heenan, who was Minister of Labour at the time, for the help he gave me on that occasion. What was the result? A year later legislation was introduced by the Minister of Labour in the Mackenzie King government regulating the wages and hours of labour of the men employed by the federal government. Thus a lead was given the provinces, and if that lead has not been followed it is not our fault. But may I say, sir, that what was done at that time by the member for Temiseouata should have been done a long time previously by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who never thought of it. He was busy reading this and that.
Well, sir, enough of that. If I were one of the electors of the constituency of Vancouver South, after listening to what my hon. friend has just said I would say to myself, " He may be sincere, but where is he going? He does not know his way." His leader, who preceded him, spoke about party capital. Does he forget that party capital is one form, perhaps the worst, of capitalism? That is what I wish to tell him. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says, "No Litvinoff,; no Russia;" he does not like us to speak about Russia or Litvinoff. I should like to see him prevent me from comparing him with Litvinoff; I should like to see him prevent me from telling him that the only difference between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and Gandhi is the goat and the spinning wheel. I am a free man, and I am here to say what I sincerely think about his policies. He comes here with a resolution so vague that he cannot explain it. That is why these hon. members have not brought in any sort of legislation to change the social order; they do not know what they want. They come with a spot-light like those who kill game in a forbidden way. They come with a spot-light to blind the eyes of the people; but God forbid that those policies ever should be adopted in Canada. They never will be, because like castles in the air they have no foundation.
These hon. gentlemen have not taken time to think over the real conditions in this country. They accept hearsay evidence all the time because they cannot form their own judgment on the facts available to them. The hon.

member for Winnipeg North Centre said he had not read the questions I put to him. I will prove, sir, that he is greatly mistaken, and to do so I need only refer to another big book, the Hansard to which I referred a few moments ago. It is a wonderful book with 2,354 pages. It is a most respectable book on account of its size, and I am sure my hon. friends in the extreme corner are delighted to have such an imposing volume shown to them. We have heard something about a change that is coming in our social system, in regard to profits. Plato published a book also, and I might tell my hon. friend from Vancouver South that Plato is a man who has been buried for quite a number of centuries. He published a book called The Republic, in which he described an ideal state, something like the lost paradise, something wonderful, but a state which never existed in the world. Let us come to Plato, who describes the state conceived by my hon. friends, but to which they have not yet given birth. It is an ideal state where no one can make profit, but where taxes will be imposed upon the people. When I asked the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who would pay for the enormous expenditures, he said that the people would. The people will have to pay for that, while making no profit. It is a mystery. And whether or not the hon. member for Vancouver South quotes Salter, or quotes or misquotes the United church or the other churches, or quotes the book he had a few moments ago the author and title of which he did not mention. I do not see how he can explain how people will be able to pay taxes to anybody if they do not have more money than is strictly required for food, for clothes, or for lodging. If they have more money than is required for those purposes, is that not profit? It would be profit. Therefore, in the state they advocate profit will be necessary, and not only profit, but a higher profit than there is now, because taxes will be higher.
How many people are to-day unable to pay the municipal taxes on their land? If one looks at the official gazette for any province he will find it is much thicker than it was before. Why? Because so many lands are being sold; people cannot pay their taxes; they have no money now. My hon. friends will advocate this garden of Allah; it is very fascinating, but it is just a cross word puzzle, a jig sa/w puzzle, something extraordinary. Under their system people will make no money, make no profit and pay more taxes. I am reminded of the story about the ship which was 300 feet long, 35 feet wide and had

Cooperative Commonwealth
a displacement of 10 feet. There were 400 people on board, together with a crew of 40. The ship had three funnels, two masts and two screws. What is the age of the captain? And, sir, I know a man who worked on that problem for two nights, and he found that the age of the captain was 56 years, 2 months, 3 days and 4 hours. I am sure that gentleman must have been either the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre or the hon. member for Vancouver South.
I have before me what was said about profit on another occasion by my hon. friends the dreamers and Utopians in the extreme corner of the house. It is different now. I can see the influence of the timid questions put by the hon. member for Temascouat-a. Here is the definition which was given on a former occasion:
A federation of organizations whose purpose is the establishment in Canada of a cooperative commonwealth in which the basic principle regulating production, distribution and exchange will be the supply of human needs instead of the making of profits.
We have heard it. When the production is greater than the consumption it should cease, automatically. My hon. friend took the same viewpoint as the Prime Minister, if we may judge toy the right hon. gentleman's action in decreasing the acreage of wheat. A decrease in production, that is it. When the production equals the consumption, it would cease automatically, and therefore people would make no profits. That is their ideal state. AVhat about exports?
But now there is a little change in the gospel of Vancouver South and Winnipeg North Centre. We find that no longer is the supply of human needs instead of the making of profits the basic principle regulating production, distribution and exchange. It is that no longer. That is no good. The social system is changed. We have a change in their own social system made by those dreamers and Utopians. They have changed it themselves. What is the necessity for the government to change the social order? Hon. members in the corner of the chamber have changed it. They have had enough of their program, the same as people have enough of a motion picture, and it has to be changed in the middle of the week. The change we now have is this:
Resolved that in the opinion of this house, since the capitalist system is failing to function in the interests of the great majority of the people of Canada, it should be superseded by a cooperative commonwealth-
Which is a euphemism for communism,
-in which the profit motive-
The profit motive-
-would be subordinated to that of public service and ruthless competition replaced by collective ownership under democratic control.
In the first place there was no making of profits,-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre may rise in his place and deny his attitude if I have not stated it correctly. He must remember what he said at other times. But he has now changed his mind. It is no longer a question of making profits. Profits are now permitted, under the autocratic rule of Winnipeg North Centre and Vancouver South. They say:
It should be superseded by a cooperative commonwealth-
Alias communism-
-in which the profit motive would be subordinated to that of public service.
Subordinated by whom? Subordinated by Winnipeg North Centre; subordinated by Vancouver South. They will be the czars of Canada; they will restore the old order of Russia. That is why they are so angry when we mention Russia. They are czarists. They believe in autocracy. They believe they are the repositories of revealed truth, and they will decree by their own powerful will that * the profit motive shall be subordinated to that of public service.
What do they mean by profit? I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to define the word "profit" and he tells me to look at the dictionary. It is not for me to look at the dictionary. The hon. member will recall the words in the Latin grammar, sapiens nihil affirmat quod non probet-the wise man does not affirm anything which he cannot prove. Those are the words of wisdom. They are not Litvinoff's; that is a maxim of truth based on the experiences of the centuries. I will tell my hon. friends, for whom I had respect until now, that if they do not clearly explain their program and their scheme-because it is only a scheme-if they do not explain it in a satisfactory way I will say that it is a contempt for the House of Commons to ask hon. members to listen to such talk as they have uttered. I will tell them that first of all they should go to the basic foundations of social life. Although not covered by section 98 of the criminal code it is really a criminal offence to deceive the Canadian people by telling them that the group in the corner of this chamber will do this, that and the other thing. Those hon. members know very well that without imposing additional taxation it would be impossible for any government to fulfil the foolish promises they
Cooperative Commonwealth

have made. It would be impossible to do what they have promised without making greater the burden of taxation which falls upon the shoulders of the good citizens of the country. I will give them one last chance. I will give them the benefit of the doubt. But, Mr. Speaker, I say they should be more serious, and when a member asks them politely for information about their own plans, which they must know, because they are supposed to have conceived them; if they will give no answer at all, I am free to form my own judgment upon them and to tell the electors in my constituency in the province of Quebec and the electors of any other constituency in this wonderful country which is Canada that these gentlemen at the extreme left of this side of the house are not serious, that they are just trying to make party capital, when telling those poor people who are suffering acutely: Follow us; we will give you anything that you wish; put us in power and see the marvels that we shall do in this country."
The candidates of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have received a minimum vote in all the by-elections since the last election. It is true that the Labour member for the city of Hamilton was elected. He visited Russia not long ago and has seen and learned about communism, and the description that he gave to the press of the conditions in Russia was entirely different from the picture which is given of the cooperative commonwealth by our friends to the extreme left. They do not even dare mention the word communism now. But you, Mr. Speaker, are a student, and if you will analyze the social system in Russia, on one hand, and the social system advocated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Vancouver South, on the other, you will see that they are one and the same thing, and that the difference is only in the name. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre is of United Empire Loyalist stock just the same as the Prime Minister of this country. He has been brought up in the British traditions of democracy, but I am sorry that he and the Prime Minister have forgotten the teachings of their youth. I regret it from the bottom of my heart. But let me tell you, sir, that although I have no English blood in my veins, just a little Irish blood-

speechtext:
Not now; nevertheless I
say that I am truer to the principles of British democracy and of British government than

my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister.
What we hear, sir, is but a deluge of words from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and his supporter the hon. member for Vancouver South-a perfect deluge of words. He says: I have compassion for the multitude. This was said by one who was not the Man of Nazareth, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre always says, but it was said by our Lord. There is not a man in this house who, unless he has a heart of stone, can listen unmoved to the sufferings of the poor, but if my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have something better to offer than the present system let them come forward boldly with public bills to amend the laws of this country. Let them tell us where there is injustice from their viewpoint. They must be familiar with the laws of this country. They often say: We are not lawyers, we are not hair-splitters. No, but there is the law maker's intent; there is the intention of the law maker, which counts; and will my hon. friends deny any responsibility for the laws which they have voted for since they have been here? What are their intentions with regard to amending or changing the social order? I hope that they will tell us that or tell us what they have done in that regard Let my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre tell us about the amendments that he has had enacted to change the social order, and then we can judge what would be the result if he could put his will into force and have his ideas enacted into law.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker; I have spoken about these hon. gentlemen for a time, and now through you I am speaking to them. I cannot speak on behalf of the government; I am against them on a matter of principle. I do not dare to speak on behalf of my party, but I can speak for myself as one who has listened to the hon. gentlemen of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and as one who has taken the trouble to read their program-which is no mean task-and to try to get something rational from it. So far as this resolution is concerned there is a missing link between the first part of their argument and the conclusion-not a missing link in the Darwinian sense, but there is a link missing just the same; and I should like to have some more explanation from them. I have put questions to them, and if I am not to receive any further explanation, then when the time comes to discuss this matter once more, or several times more, whether in this house or out of it, we will tell the people

Cooperative Commonwealth
that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Vancouver South were not serious and were just playing politics when they brought in their resolution about the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. The people of this country in an indignant mood will tell them: You are not going to fool us any more; and then the candidates of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation will not receive even a minority vote, or enough votes to give a chance to any Tory candidate to be elected.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a resolution similar to the present one but not exactly the same was moved in this house in 1932 and another in 1933. I believe the resolutions of 1932 and 1933 were identical. But when the resolution was moved again in 1934 there was a change in it, and there is a change again now in 1935. I opposed the former resolutions and I rise to oppose this resolution also. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in his address took a good deal to his party when he described the mayor of Toronto as a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation mayor. The mayor of Toronto is a capable gentleman with a great deal of ability, but in the last election, like Joseph, he wore a coat of many colours, one of which was the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. In his support were many well known and staunch Conservatives and many well known and staunch Liberals, and his principal support came as I understand it from the independent Labour party. So the hon. member cannot claim the mayor of Toronto as an out and out C.C.F'er.
The hon. member quoted many articles from the press in which he purported to show that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had denounced the capitalist system. Well, I listened very attentively to the Prime Minister in all his speeches except the first one; I was not at home on that occasion and had not the pleasure of hearing the speech as it was delivered, but I read it carefully afterwards. My memory is that he denounced the abuses and the violations that had crept into the system and intimated that he and his government would reform the system and cut out the abuses.
The hon. member said further that nobody wanted to abolish capitalists, but I cannot see where that coincides with the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, which was apparently adopted again on February 10, and one item of which reads that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes that capitalism can be neither
reformed nor restored. So that if capitalism is to 'be wiped out, of course capitalists go with it. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) said that the program advocated by this resolution of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had not been changed; but I find a change in the resolutions that have been moved except the first two. In 1932 the expression is used "a large number of" in referring to the people, and in the present resolution it says "great majority." In the resolution of 1934 the word "masses" is used whereas, as I say, in the present resolution the people are referred to as the great majority.
I find a slight swinging to the right in the present resolution as compared with the former, because in the present resolution we have the words "by a cooperative commonwealth in which the profit motive would be subordinated to that of public service." Subordinated merely means being on a lower plane. This is the first resolution my hon. friends have moved in which, I take it, from the resolution itself, there is some justification of the profit motive; otherwise the word "subordinated" would not be there but perhaps there would be the words "wiped out " and in that regard it would be on a par with the former resolutions. There is, I say, a swinging just a little to the right from the extreme left position of a few years ago, and in this the mover of the resolution and those supporting him are in line with what is being done in Russia. There is a slight move in Russia towards the right. I have here an associated press dispatch from Moscow under date December 30, 1934, quoting one who I presume is the head of the republic, the Hon. Joseph Stalin, in an address to the metallurgical group of industry. Apparently the iron and steel industry is not making that headway which it would like to see, although it is making progress, and to encourage the men working in the plants producing iron and steel to do betteT Joseph Stalin is quoted as using the slogan, "Technique without men is dead." And further down:
Higher pay for efficient technical men was one of the means Stalin suggested to directors of the Soviet iron and steel industries for improvement of their technique.
"Organize wages so they will strengthen the decisive links of production and prompt people on to higher skill," Stalin urged. "This is what we need in order to create a large army of industrial technical cadres."
That is quite a move to the right, because in all the arguments that have come out of Russia we were given to understand that there was to be equal pay for similar work. So that
Cooperative Commonwealth

we find them swinging slightly to the right over there; and our friends in the opposite corner, leaving in their resolution the two words "profit motive," merely putting it on a lower plane, are also swinging slightly to the right.
Reading over the resolution, and remembering what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) said in the press- it may not have been a correct report-giving his views in endorsing some if not all of the proposals of the Prime Minister in his radio addresses, I thought that if a resolution were moved by the opposite corner this session it would be more or less in these words. This is just a suggested resolution: "Resolved, that in the opinion of this house, since the capitalistic system has been prevented from functioning as it should do in the interests of the people of Canada, as a result of the failure of governments in past years to stop the introduction of the abuse and gross violation of its true principles, this house endorses the courage of the present government in its projected legislation designed to eradicate and cut out the abuses and violations of the capitalistic system and supports its determination, at this session, to enact the necessary remedial legislation to achieve in the best interests of the people this laudable objective." That would be very good and to the point.
This is my fifth session in this house and I have yet to hear-or I cannot remember having heard, I will put it that way-any constructive suggestion from the opposite corner of this house looking to the providing of sound employment for the unemployed. We have had several speeches to-night, one or two at any rate from the opposite corner, and not one thing has been said in the way of providing sound employment for the large number of unemployed in the country. Before I sit down I shall try to show what the government has done in that regard and what it proposes to do. Let me refer first of all to Count Nicholas Ignatieff, an exiled Russian nobleman, now a professor in Lansing, Michigan. Speaking at Orillia to the Canadian Institute on Economics and Politics, he made two or three significant statements in reference to Russia and the cooperative system in vogue there. He said:
The peasants fought collectivization desperately and almost fought the government to a standstill. They slaughtered stock, destroyed grain and starved themselves rather than submit.
What does it mean? Just this: collective man is the latest product of man's hallucinations-
I believe the hon. gentleman who just sat down referred to something that was said a3

being like an hallucination. This is from a Russian nobleman who knows what hallucinations are:
-there is no such thing. Man is primarily individual and his happiness and his most important functions are individual.
If this country is to have inflicted upon it- if that is the proper word-the abolition of the capitalistic system and to have substituted for it cooperative commonwealthism, then individualism will be destroyed. My experience over a long period in association with many thousands of men, observing them work and produce from their heads many splendid and successful inventions, has convinced me that if you eliminate the opportunity of the human race to aspire to produce and to conceive ideas and profit therefrom, you will eliminate from this world much of that which is to its advantage. Continuing, Count Ignatieff says:
True cooperation starts with the individual. The right to private property is recognized. The individual is free to do whatever he will with his share of his earnings, accumulate wealth and leave it to his children.
Collectivism, on the other hand, seeks to submerge the individual in the swarm, in the herd-it negates every aspect of individualism and recognizes no human inequalities. It sets up the tyranny of the swarm over the individual.
But as I said at the outset, there is a slight wheel from the doctrine of "all are equal in Russia" to the doctrine that those who labour hardest and produce the most shall receive some extra consideration for their efforts.
I am not one of those who believe the cause of all our troubles is the capitalistic system, but I do believe what I understood the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to say in his radio addresses, namely, that the abuses and violations of the capitalistic system are partly if not wholly responsible for the troubles through which we are passing. The capitalistic system is founded on sound doctrine. We all know the fourth commandment refers to the fact that man shall work not more than six days a week. Well, legislation that is before the house this session is designed to provide one day of rest each week for all workmen, and in that particular the capitalist system of this country is going back to that principle and that doctrine of the fourth commandment.
Another principle of the capitalist system is the practice of thrift, and here again we are encouraged by the _Holy Book to practise thrift. I have in mind the parable of the talents: three different servants were each given talents; one buried his, the second doubled his and the third increased his five to ten, and on the return of the lord of those

Cooperative Commonwealth
servants the latter two were commended for their thrift. The practice of thrift is one of the doctrines of the capitalist system, and I do not know how thrift is to be incorporated in the theories advanced by hon. gentlemen in the far corner Who are sponsoring this resolution.
Then we have another doctrine of the capitalist system-the reward for labour. I am in accord with that; I believe those who work hardest should receive the most; that is if two are labouring in the same line of business or profession, the man who is willing to deny himself and work hard is surely entitled to consideration for his determination to advance in his work.
Then we have the doctrine of the reward for skill. Why should a man not be rewarded for his skill? In support of this we have the head of the Russian state arguing before a group of iron and steel manufacturers in Russia that they too must depart from their former doctrine of equality of men to a doctrine of reward to those who do the most, achieve the most and produce the most.
Another principle of the capitalistic system is that individual effort should receive consideration, another, that men should live uprightly. I am strongly in accord with that, that those who live uprightly and endeavour to do the most good in this world, do the most for humanity.
Then we have the doctrine to treat others as we would be treated. Well, there have been violations of all those doctrines or principles. It has not been a question of violation this year or last year, but it has been a question for years of progressive violation, progressive abuse of the capitalistic system. On Friday night last when on the debate in connection with introducing the eight hour day we were told by those who opposed the resolution that this government could not bring about the eight hour day; that that, so they alleged, and other kindred subjects are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Perhaps that is one of the reasons, the fact that there are nine provinces and nine provincial governments, why the capitalistic system has been violated and abused in this country as it has been.
Then we have the further doctrine of being honest and paying our accounts. When the Pharisees, seeking to tempt Our Lord in reference to money matters, asked Him if they should pay tribute to Caesar, He asked them to show Him a coin. He then asked them whose image and superscription was on the coin, and they told him that it was Caesar's; whereupon He said to them: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's." The trouble is that in this country and, indeed, throughout the world, accounts have not been paid that should have been paid. These and many other doctrines followed by the capitalist system have been violated and abused. Along come the government of the day proposing reforms. They have the courage and the determination bo do it, and the Prime Minister in his addresses said that he would remove abuses. I believe he will, and I believe the house will support his legislation to do away with the violations and abuses of capitalism. If a ship sails the seas for years without 'being taken into dry dock it will become covered with barnacles; therefore ships are taken into dry dock periodically and the barnacles scraped off. We should not condemn the ship because it did not travel as wrell 'before the barnacles were scraped off as after. The capitalistic system is cluttered up with a lot of barnacles of one kind and another; this government is going to scrape them off, and the abuses and violations will be eliminated.
