subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext:
Plug it. In 1932 a committee of the United States senate investigated one of the great abuses of the capitalistic system that is, stock market abuses, which prevailed, incidentally, not in the United States only but in Canada as well. It was not investigated in Canada, and that is why I refer to the United States investigation. These were nothing short of outrageous and never should have been permitted. But we cannot say that the capitalistic system was responsible for that. Now they have been eliminated, and the government of that country is to be congratulated upon what it has done in that regard. I shall give one example of the gross abuse of the capitalistic system that took place there, and no doubt there w'ere similar cases in Canada also. The committee reported that stocks were boosted by false statements, that the public were rigged-that was one of the most outrageous abuses practised on the public. Then there were bear raids, bull raids, short selling and long selling, and stock splits. I have read of stocks that were split not opce or twice but four, five, six, seven, and eight times, without any new capital being added. That is a violation of the capitalistic system, and never should have been permitted. I am sure this government will deal with any situation like that if it has control of the matter and the provinces do not act. Then there were wash
Cooperative Commonwealth

sales, and selling against the box, and buying and selling at the same time. In 1929, when the first crash came, stocks on the New York stock exchange shrank $29,000,000,000, and in 1930, there was an additional fall of $20,000,000,000, or a total of $49,000,000,000 within a year. Stock promoters and market manipulators never should have been permitted so to violate the principles of honesty, thrift and fair play that are the foundations of the capitalistic system. However, the government of the United States have enacted new legislation designed to prevent such exploitation in the future. Think of Radio stock, which in 1921 stood at $105,000,000; in 1929, without addition of further capital, rose to $1,400,000.000; and in 1930 after the crash it dropped to $175,000,000, a shrinkage of $1,225,000,000. That was an example of the great abuses and violations of the capitalistic system, but abuses of the kind will be eliminated both across the line and in this country. I hope the Canadian governments will rise to the occasion and by whatever methods they may adopt prevent in future any such stock exploitation as has taken place in the past. Of course the stock market people offer the defence that during the war people were educated to buy bonds and stocks, money was plentiful and people learned to buy, and that is one of the causes that made this exploitation possible. But the governments of this country must enact legislation to prevent this and other abuses of the capitalistic system.
Then there are other violations; sweat shops-the Prime Minister has already announced that he will eliminate sweat shops. Some may say he has not the power; but I doubt very much if any hon. member will oppose the elimination of sweat shops or oppose giving the government power to eliminate them. Sweat shops are not a necessary part of the capitalistic system; they are a violation of the system and never should have been permitted to exist. Neither should the seven day working week. The government hv its eight hour day and forty-eight hour week legislation is going to stop such abuses. Then as to mergers, I do not say that in no case should mergers be allowed, but there were altogether too many of them; the great flood of mergers was not a legitimate feature of the capitalistic system but a violation of it.
Then will anyone say that the outrageous waste, not only in Canada but in the republic to the south, such as the slaughter in the United States of several million hogs, the destruction of millions of acres of com and

cotton, was any true part of the capitalistic system? They were violations of it. We all know, too, that the great war was responsible for much of our trouble. Certainly the abolition of war is the desire of every hon. member of this house, but I cannot understand how war can be attributed wholly to the capitalistic system; I call it a heinous violation of the system.
Then we have rampant partyism. This parliament is in its fifth session; during its life the country has been going through the worst depression in the world's history, and I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite will admit that the government has at least done its best to bring the country through. Yet how often have we found them forgetting partyism and rallying to the support of legislation enacted for the advancement of this country? Surely partyism should not be carried to such a length that we must denounce everything that our opponents advance. Surely our opponents are sometimes right, and when that is so I believe in admitting it.
What do the government propose in order to eliminate the abuses of the capitalistic system that now exist? We have the proposed establishment of the eight hour day, one day's rest in seven, and unemployment insurance. Someone said something about unemployment insurance to-day; when that resolution is under discussion again I propose to speak on it, but for the moment I will content myself with saying that in spite of what has been said the unemployment insurance measure will do a great deal of good and will fill a long felt want in this country. In addition we have proposals along the lines of national health, controlled speculation and minimum wages; it is proposed to abolish sweatshops, and finally steps have been taken by the government to provide work. One of the hon. members from Winnipeg said the government was not doing anything to provide employment. I devote a good deal of my time to matters pertaining to labour; in the course of the recess I come in contact with many hundreds of men who are employed in industry, and I speak without fear of successful contradiction when I say that the government has done a very great deal, through legislation, to provide new employment in this country. The government has not received very much support in that regard from hon. members in the far corner, among others, but it has enacted legislation that has resulted in a great deal of new employment.

Cooperative Commonwealth
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre returned from a trip to Japan he gave an interview, which appeared in the Toronto Mail and Empire of January 14. The hon. gentleman is reported as decrying Japanese cheap labour, and as saying that Japanese goods are cheap partly because of low labour standards but largely because of downright efficiency. If we pass the resolution now before the house, in what way shall we be protecting Canadian workmen against either Japanese efficiency or Japanese cheap labour? As the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said, we have to deal with realities; we have to look at things as they are, and we have to consider our country in the light of what is going on in all other countries. Certainly this is no time for Canada to take up some new-fangled idea, or rather an old idea revamped. With the serious situation in which we find ourselves this is a time when we must face things as they are and look at realities, and certainly I cannot see how any resolution such as this will help the situation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that resolutions similar to this have been before the house on four or five occasions previously. I think if I had moved a resolution that had been thrown out by the house four or five times, I would not bother introducing it again.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CAPITALISTIC SYSTEM BE SUPER-SEDEJ) BY A SOCIAL ORDER IN WHICH THE PROFIT MOTIVE WOULD BE SUBORDINATED TO PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it a tragedy that we should have such discussion as has taken place within the last hour and a half; it would indicate a failure to appreciate the Prime Minister's words, "the crash and thunder of toppling capitalism."
The previous speaker (Mr. MacNicol) dealt with the alleged reforms of the present government and expressed regret that there was not more wholehearted support from this section of this house in regard to that legislation. He asked, "Why do we not look at facts and realities?" In his speech he did not face one fact or one reality; he did not even approach a consideration of the problem. We have misery, destitution, poverty, and unemployed millions here and throughout the world. We have a hopeless outlook for youth with education of no value, so far as entrance to the economic field is concerned, and the government comes along with shreds and patches that have been tried out in other capitalist countries, and which have left them in the same morass that we are in. Yet the government wonders why we are not enthusiastic about the program.
They tell us that prosperity is returning, and that therefore this legislation is going to be all right. Again they do not face facts or estimate realities. The Wall Street Journal of comparatively recent date points out that in the first six months profits in 56 industrial corporations of the larger type had increased by 174-6 per cent over the previous six months. That looked like returning prosperity, and my hon. friend who has just sat down would so describe it. Hon. gentlemen opposite and to my right would describe it as such, and would be content to place that fact before the public. Continue; analyze a little closer, and you find that while profits increased by 174-6 per cent sales increased by only 51 per cent. In other words profits increased three times as fast as sales. Exactly the same thing is taking place in Canada and has begun to take place in Great Britain. It has been accompanied by this further phenomenon, that whilst profits and sales increased, wages continued to go down. At the very time the Wall Street Journal published the statement to which I made reference, Miss Perkins, Secretary of Labour for the United States of America, had the great courage to publish a statement relating to the situation. In that statement, with the official imprimatur of the Department of Labour, she stated that during that period factory payrolls went down 6-8 per cent, or a decline on the average of $10,460,000 a week. So we find profits going up at the expense of the wage earning and producing classes.
How long do hon. gentlemen think their system can continue with that going on? How long can they hope to carry on a system that shows such a mad, illogical, untenable and uneconomic condition? But that is not all. This government now proposes legislation which already either in part or in whole has been adopted in other countries. Yes, in whole-all of it has been adopted in many countries, such as Great Britain. A far wider experimentation has taken place in the United States. It is of value to us to-night to consider just what the results have been in the United States, in order to ascertain whether or not we may draw conclusions therefrom. I would suggest that the last speaker (Mr. MacNicol)

it would be of no use to suggest it to the one who preceded him (Mr. Pouliot)-should analyse what has taken place in the United States under what is called the new deal. The actual level of wages in that country in July, 1934, was up 8-5 per cent as compared with the level in July, 1933, followed, as Miss Perkins noted, by a decline. However they were up at one
Cooperative Commonwealth

stage, and we shall deal with that picture for the moment. Wages were up 8-5 per cent. Prices during the same period were up 9-6 per cent. At a moment's consideration hon. members will realize that the effect is obvious. The net effect is that the purchasing power was decreased 1-1 per cent. Surely that was not the purpose of the new deal; I believe its purpose was the very reverse. In my view it was the sincere intention of the government of the United States, just as I believe it to be the sincere intention of this government, to increase the standard of living and the purchasing power of the people. But under the present system it cannot be done. It has been tried out in the United States to a far greater degree than this country proposes to try it, and in that country it has failed.
These actual figures dealing with the purchasing power of the American middle class are significant, and I ask hon. members to take them into serious consideration. In 1933 the incomes of the middle class ranging from less than $10,000-a substantial sum-down to nothing were decreased by five per cent as compared with their revenues in 1932. On the other hand individuals having incomes of a million dollars or more per year saw an increase in revenues ranging from twenty to forty-six per cent. An analysis shows that while in the aggregate middle class incomes were being reduced, higher incomes were being enormously increased. Surely that was not the intention of the new deal. Yet that was the effect of the attempt to regulate capitalism-and we will find that the same results will follow in this country under the present proposals.
I turn now for a moment to a consideration of conditions in Europe. What is the lesson we may learn from the experiments over there? In western Europe general industrial production, despite the rigid state regulations of many nations is about fifteen per cent less than it was in 1913, and in addition to that fact we must consider the further one, namely that between 1913 and to-day there has been an enormous increase in population. Therefore in Europe they had an increase in population together with a fifteen per cent decrease in production. Capitalism has not justified its existence, has it? Regulation has not shown effective results, has it? In 1922 fascism came into existence in Italy, and at that time many promises were made to the masses of the people. In 1933 the wage rate in Italy was seventeen per cent less than it was in 1929, and unemployment
[Mr. E. J. Garland.!
had increased from 293,000 to 1,057,000. That is a fact worth while considering. And so we find that- fascism has not separated Italy from the general capitalist collapse which has affected all the world. We should profit from their twelve years of experience. In Germany since 1930 the workers have suffered a decline in wages averaging sixty-three per cent, and the decline is said to be worse among the agricultural classes. In that time the level of the so-called upper classes has remained relatively constant in all those countries. Yet we propose to patch and scratch in this country.
Yes, you know, people do draw conclusions, very final conclusions, from very strange premises. I was frankly amused when I read in a newspaper what purported to be a report of an alleged interview with the Prime Minister while in England not long ago. He is quoted as follows:
I was delighted in London to see such evidence of increasing prosperity.
Evidence of increasing prosperity.
Well dressed people on the streets, crowds in the shops, and the spirit everywhere apparently indicated that England is leaving the depression behind her.
Yes, and that same day I walked down the main street of the city of Calgary. I saw well dressed people on the streets; I saw them in the shops; I even saw individuals smoking cigars; I saw ladies and gentlemen 'greeting each other with smiles, but I did not come to the conclusion that prosperity had returned. Did the Prime Minister take the trouble to examine the broken industries of Bradford? Did he go to Lancashire? Did he go out to the slums of Stratford east and Bow road? Did he look at the herds of hopelessness in England? Did he listen even to the Prime Minister of England who about that time said that there were millions who never again would be employed, millions whom Ramsay MacDonald described as "human scrap"? Of course those people will never be reemployed under capitalism. It cannot be done. There is no place for them any more than there is for our youth, under capitalism. Did the Prime Minister take the trouble or has any hon. member who assumes a returning prosperity simply because profits have gone up in spots taken the trouble, to ascertain the fact that in Lancashire there are 16,000,000 idle spindles, and that a committee appointed by the British government has been investigating the matter? Do they know that the committee has already made an interim report in which they propose scrapping 7,000,000 spindles? That is a recom-

Cooperative Commonwealth
mendation to create an artificial scarcity, such as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maolnnis) has described. Unless we create a scarcity capitalism cannot continue. Unless the Canadian people and the people of the world are to be content with a lower standard of living, this present system can neither be regulated nor continued.
Sometimes institutions which have their very foundations in the system unwittingly confess its total and absolute failure. The insurance companies of Canada are supposed to be the sheet anchors of capitalism, the sheet anchors of the thrifty, and all that sort of stuff. In order to get business they advertise extensively in the newspapers. In 1928, when there was what is termed a capitalist boom, one of those insurance companies published an advertisement in the Canadian newspapers in an endeavour to secure the money of thrifty investors. The Canada Life Assurance Company asks the question-and here we see the appeal to fear, the psychology of modern advertising: "What happens to one hundred average men of twenty-five years of age upon reaching the age of sixty-five?" Out of the vast compilation of statistics that are at their disposal as a result of their actuarial research covering many years, they are able to make this accurate statement, and no one questions it; no one has counter-statistics to offset it: One of the hundred will be wealthy; four will be well to do and able to enjoy some comfort and recreation; five will be still working for a living, with no prospect of relief from drudgery; fifty-four will be dependent upon friends or relatives or charity; and thirty-six will be dead. So to one hundred young men of twenty-five years of age this intelligent, highly to be appreciated capitalist system has nothing better to offer, even in days of prosperity so-called, than that four out of the hundred will have some security in old age; five will be still working for a living with no hope of escape from drudgery at the age of sixty-five, and the remainder of the one hundred will be either dead or relying upon friends or relatives or charity. If there be hon. members of this house who desire to sustain a system so self-condemned as that, frankly I cannot understand their mentality or their logic, and I dissociate myself from them.
I pick up statistics of this government's own departments, data available to every member of the house, and I find facts that should shock hon. gentlemen of this house even if the investigations before the mass buying committee have not sufficiently done so. I find, for example, in a census bulletin published under authority of Hon. H. H. Stevens,
Minister of Trade and Commerce, a departmental bulletin entitled, Earnings Among Wage Earners for Canada and the Provinces, the following facts.
In the coal mining industry in my province there are employed 5,474 persons, and their average annual earnings according to the bulletin amount to $652. They are employed 27-51 weeks-27 weeks-out of the year. But, you see, the poor devils have to eat for fifty-two weeks, and they have to clothe themselves and pay rent and light and fuel and all the other things for the whole year; and so we find that they had to live fifty-two weeks on an average of $12.50 a week, or $1.78 a day. Is it suggested they ought to be very enthusiastic about the system? Would I if I were in their position be hurrahing for it and for those tinkering with it until even the Prime Minister would be gratified?
Now take the earnings of all wage earners in Canada. According to this same bulletin, pages 12 and 13, I find that the average yearly earnings for all employed in Canada is S743. Male earners secured on the average $927, and female earners S560. By the way, it is a significant thing that in this interesting man made system of ours you will find, if you check the figures, that in every case the women work more weeks and usually longer hours and in every case receive less pay than the men.

Take another side of the picture. Keep in mind, please, the figures I have just given, the average yearly earnings of $743. I wrote to the Department of Labour to ascertain what they regard as an adequate annual budgetary maintenance, and I find that by the industrial relations committee a few years ago an investigation was made into this question and a compilation made by the
Cooperative Commonwealth

bureau; the Labour department have brought the figures up to date to August, 1934, and they are as follows:
To maintain a poverty level of existence in Canada you require $661.16 per year. A minimum subsistence level would require, according to the department, $1,069.16. But the average earnings per year in Canada are only $743. Therefore the average earnings in Canada are less, by nearly $300, than the minimum subsistence level set out in the tables of the Department of Labour. The health and decency level is $1,328; and the comfort level $1,867.
Now contributory unemployment insurance, taking into consideration all these facts, can only bring you to the conclusion that its chief effect will be to reduce at least during this time the available purchasing power of tht masses of the people. I am not opposed to it for that reason, but I just desire to point out facts, especially to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat. If these poor beggars have to carry on with average earnings per year of $743 and are expected to pay any contribution at all, it can only lessen the total volume of purchasing power and in the long run have but little effect. Certainly it can have no other effect until there is another depression, if we ever get out of the present one, and we are not out of it yet.
Then we have the other side of the picture. The concentration of the control of the means of life is one of the major developments of the last century under this capitalist system Everybody admits that to-day, and everybody is beginning to apologize for it, including the last speaker. The Mellon family, for example, a family that conducts business in Canada as well as in the United States of America, provides probably one of the best examples of how wealth, and with it the destinies of millions of people, have been concentrated in a few hands. While the masses of the people were suffering in the penurious condition I have stated, this family fortune was being built up until to-day the Mellon family has a fortune estimated at eight billions of dollars, or, to be exact, $7,990,425,178. Now, that is a pretty substantial fortune. That is capitalism. That is capitalism because it gave the opportunity to a predatory type to take the fullest and grossest advantage of the system that encouraged predatory characters.
I would like my hon. friend who made some reference to the fourth commandment, or something like that, to take that into consideration. The whole philosophy of competition is contrary to Christ and to the teachings of Christ, and the very principle
[Mr. E. J. Garland.)
of competition in a capitalist society is utterly incompatible with the teachings of Him to whom he referred.
Then take even their own newspapers. Just about Christmas time this advertisement appeared on behalf of the Calgary Albertan, published in the city in which the right hon. the Prime Minister represents the west riding:
It said:
Feeding many on little. Is this your problem? The Albertan will help you solve it. Economical but nourishing and attractive meals can be prepared for your family cheaply. We will show you how to prevent waste; how to make tasteful meals from cheaper commodities; how to utilize to the utmost all the food properties of your provisions.
Yet at that moment we were selling cattle at destructive prices to a government in order that they might be turned into fertilizer. But our capitalist newspapers will advertise, in the face of that, this sort of thing to unfortunates who are expected to live on an average of five cents per meal on relief in our cities-advertising how they may be able to put life into their bodies by economizing in those things of which to-day we are able to produce in such vast abundance. Just think of the stupidity of the system. Does anyone think that these things can be remedied by regulation? There comes to my mind one classical illustration which I heard not long ago from a gentleman whom the Prime Minister has quoted, certainly without disagreeing with him, so far as I could ascertain from the newspapers. I refer to Mr. John Strachey, who told this interesting story in my hearing. One of the best illustrations of the insanity of the present system is to be found in the experience which two countries in Europe have recently had. In order to relieve unemployment conditions in Holland the government of that country decided to start great public works with a view to employing the unemployed, and the object of these public works was the reclamation of the Zuyder Zee. They were to erect dykes and drain the water off the land They had previously ascertained that the land itself was fertile and would be productive, and so they employed their unemployed. After the land had been restored they placed the unemployed on it, producing. They then found that they were producing so much wheat that they created a surplus wheat condition in the local market, and the government that had encouraged the development of that enterprise was then compelled in turn to buy the surplus wheat. Having bought the surplus wheat they attempted to find a market and, not being able to find one at remunerative prices, they finally sold the

Cooperative Commonwealth
wheat at cost to the Danish government in order that it should be fed to hogs there. The Danish government fed it to the hogs, with the result that there was an increase in the production of hogs, which threatened the market; and to avoid the collapse of the hog market the government of Denmark took over the surplus hogs. They could not tell what to do with these hogs and so they in turn converted the hogs into fertilizer. Then, finding that Denmark was so well provided with productive land and that production was so high, they had no market for their fertilizer in Denmark but succeeded in selling it back to Holland, so that they could spread it on the reclaimed Zuyder Zee to create more wheat to feed more hogs to be converted into more fertilizer, and so on. That is capitalism. My friends do not like it. They speak of the sacredness of the home, while around them they see their own people daily dispossessed of their homes, daily evicted from their homes. And who owned those homes-the home dwellers? You will find an exact parallel in other countries to the situation I now portray to you. I take four of the leading industrial states of the United States and according to a census of recent years we find that there were 4,828,000 dwellings in those four states, and of that number 4,115,000 were rented. Did private initiative, private enterprise and courageous loyalty to capitalism enable those people to buy homes and hold them?
Mr. Speaker, this movement, to which I have the honour to belong, has for its purpose the establishment of the sanctity of true private property and its extension, and we seek to have every person own his own home as an inalienable right and not as a matter of sufferance or charity. And it can be done. We have the man power, the scientific attainments, the artificial power, the raw materials, the willingness to work and the capital-it is all there. All you have to do is to bring these things into harmony. Capitalism lived-for I think it is dead-so long as the workers were able to feed the capitalists. But capitalism failed, to use the mildest term, just so soon as the capitalists had begun to feed the workers; and the more the capitalist has to feed the workers the more certain it is that the destruction of the system has been accomplished.
The proposed unemployment legislation is to make the workers feed the capitalists and their unemployed brethren as well. That is what this type of unemployment insurance does. It makes the employed feed the capitalists-for they will always pass on their costs to the consumer-and in addition to that
the employed has to feed his unemployed brethren. You cannot solve an economic problem of this magnitude by anything of that sort. It cannot be done, and that is so obvious that one does not need to stress it.
Hon. gentlemen to my immediate right believe, as I myself believed for many years, that all the present horrible muddled condition can be remedied if only we will restore the free market, free, unregulated competition. If only we will do that, they think, everything will be splendid. Well, I have changed my views in that regard; I no longer believe that position to be either tenable or possible of attainment. To do this, let us find out what we should have to do. We should have first to restore the normal flow of commodities by levelling the tariff and by the reversal of the policy of administrative protection-in othei words, world free trade or as near an approach thereto as possible. Secondly, it would be incumbent upon any government holding these views to break down the trusts and monopolies, for they interfere with the free movement of internal exchange just as effectively as tariffs interfere with the international movement of goods. Next, they would have to reverse the entire tendency towards the establishment of social services and of state and trade union protection for the wage earner; for social services and static wages are progressively freezing one of the most important variables of the law of supply and demand. In fact restoration of the free markets in labour would have to be accomplished if restoration of the system were to be accomplished. In addition, it would be incumbent upon them to establish some form of monetary control on a world scale which can attempt-and I use the word "attempt" advisedly-the task of mitigating world crises. In fact, restoration of the stability and continuity of international exchange must be accomplished if those hon. gentlemen are to make good their protestations. How could those reforms be brought about, even if they were advisable, in our present developed state of society? How are you going to level or diminish the existing tariff barriers of the world? Who is to do those jobs?-for if those tariffs are disastrous to the world market as a whole, they are of enormous benefit to particular capitalists. In short, the general enrichment that free trade would bring about could be achieved only at the cost of a gigantic redistribution of wealth among both individuals and communities. Individual capitalists would be ruined and whole industrial sections laid desolate. The free trader given power to scale down tariffs will also by that act be given power to bestow great

Cooperative Commonwealth
wealth, to deal destruction here, to bring ruin there, and so he will be opposed by every powerful and organized force of the entrepreneurs of every state fighting for existence. Try to do this, Mr. Speaker.
Second, they have to break the trusts. Who will inform the Holts, the Mellons and the others that they have to divest themselves of their present privileges and relinquish them to the will of the state? Why, as somebody suggests, there might be a great difficulty in securing campaign funds in the next election, if such action were taken.

Next, the free traders must, having challenged the greatest interests in capitalism, proceed to take away from the workers everything they have gained in a century of organized effort. It is of little use to restore freedom of exchange of commodities both internationally and at home and leave trade in one vital commodity, human labour, hedged about by every restriction and restraint. The
[Mr. E. J. Garland.)
free market can operate successfully and automatically only when all its interconnecting parts are movable; for if one of those parts sticks, the whole jams. It therefore would be essential that the price of human labour should vary freely in its relation to supply and demand. Further, as some social services provide, through the intervention of the state, income for labour in addition to that secured by wages, the existence of the legislation definitely retards the tendency of the price of labour to find its natural level; and hence it is important of course to the free trader that all such gross interferences with the freedom of the market, such as trade boards, old age pensions, health insurance and other forms of direct contribution by the state should cease. No laissez-faire system, no system of free competition could continue.
Finally comes the need of establishing international monetary control in order to prevent the wild fluctuations in international exchange that will hamper the movement of commodities in a free world market. The establishment of such a monetary control implies inevitably the setting up of a super power international in character, a bank that would have such control as to be able to determine the necessary steps and controls to be taken in order to regulate all exchange rates as between nations so as to avoid any clog in the system. Obviously that is incompatible with national sovereignty. So world tariff levelling, world tariff trust-busting, world trade union smashing and finally the inducing of French bankers, United States senators and all those other people to deposit their gold in some central bank in Geneva or wherever it is thought convenient, is the pleasant task of the free trader.
The system is gone and we might as well realize it. When we do we shall turn our efforts to the setting up of a cooperative social system in this country that will enable the harmonious functioning of the factors I mentioned earlier, man power, artificial power, resources and factory equipment, in order that we may be able to satisfy fully the needs of the people of Canada.

failed and is continuing to fail, how does he hope to succeed? How does he hope to persuade the people of Canada that his leader, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), can save the nation? With a gesture of contempt he said, "How long will this system go on?" I tell my hon. friend that this system existed before he was born, and it will continue to exist long after he is dead and gone, after every one of us is dead and gone. His leader spoke about the necessity for something new, as if he were espousing a new cause. Years ago when I was a student at Queen's university we learned that Plato talked about socialism and communism. Why, this is as old as mankind; it is a relic of society in its most primitive form-it is not new. The hon, mem ber spoke about the purpose of the new dea' in the United States; he said it was to increase purchasing power. They poured out billions and billions and are pouring out billions still in the United States; and have they increased purchasing power? He sa3rs they have not. What then is his alternative? The hon. member is perfectly right when he says that there are conditions existing in society which are absolutely cruel. No one can approve of a system that alternates from the peaceful pursuits of civilization to the savagery of war; certainly we agree with his condemnation of the system. But what is his alternative?

Not content with analyzing the situation in the great republic to the south, our eloquent friend took us on a Cook's tour through Europe. He spoke about Italy and gave statistics regarding wage reductions there. Are he and his companions greater than Mussolini? "Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed that he is grown so great?" This is a question I might reasonably ask of the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot). If he were in the house now I would ask him if he would kindly invite me to dinner before I rise again to address the house. I imagine he must feed upon dynamite.

It is dynamite to
some of the Liberal party I am afraid, or perhaps even nitroglycerine and gun cotton.
But let us take a look at Europe. Look at the situation in Russia. I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will pardon my making reference to Russia, because I have never classified my hon. friend as a revolutionist. I believe the hon. member who leads the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is a man of the highest motives. I believe he is a great idealist. I believe the suffering of humanity has so deeply marked his heart that he cannot forget it. I believe that his purpose in this house and throughout his life is to make the bread of life a little sweeter for the poor, if I may put it that way. I also believe that there are many men in this house who have the same ideal, even men in the Conservative party. But when I analyze this resolution I realize the lack of logic in it. Let me read the resolution in order that we may see just how much truth it contains. It is very much like the Declaration of Independence, which started with a lie, that all men are created free and equal. I think that was one of the most poetic lies ever penned by our political philosophers. The hon. member says in his resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, since the capitalist system is failing to function in the interests of the great majority of the people of Canada-[DOT]
When you postulate the fact that the system is failing to function in the insterests of the great majority of the people you mean that more than half of the people of Canada are in a condition approaching destitution or poverty, and I do not think that is correct. There is enough suffering in Canada, God knows, without starting your resolution with an exaggerated statement which, upon its face, certainly is not true.

When we talk about the failure of the capitalistic system I wonder if we ever recognize its virtues and merits. What has the capitalistic system done for us? It has lessened hours of labour; it has lightened the drudgery of toil; it has harnessed the power that is leaping in the cataracts and the rivers. The other day, as I looked at the river here and saw that magic array of lights along the shore, I was thinking that if an Indian who, living in the north in seclusion, and not having heard of the inventions of modern society and the great privileges we now possess, came down the river and saw this array of lights, he would think the stars had fallen from heaven and were dancing up and down upon the hills. The capitalistic system has done nothing? Even in this House of Commons the capitalistic system has permitted the great amount of freedom and liberty. It has enabled you and me, men bom of poor parents and without monetary resources or power, to come here in the name of the people and, in the temple of the people, to speak against all the power that ever was or ever will be with the voice of freedom and love. There is no good in the capitalistic system? Look back to the days of Queen Elizabeth. Remember how they lived then, when they had no sanitation, when they had not discovered glass, when there was practically no pottery or porcelain, when they knew nothing about the modem science of medicine; when they feasted and drank together in palaces in which there was nothing but a litter of straw for a carpet, where they flung their despised bones to the dogs. To-day I, a mechanic's son, and you, are rich, with more freedom and more luxury than Queen Elizabeth on her throne ever had or ever dreamed of having.
I remember once, when I was a lad, looking at Eaton's catalogue. That was a long time ago; Eaton's have been in existence for a long time, like the capitalistic system. I was about six years of age, and I remember that on the cover of the catalogue there was a picture of the horseless carriage. I looked at my aunt and said, "Is that a horseless carriage, Aunt Laura?" She said, "Yes, Jim." My hon. friend said the Prime Minister does not know the meaning of words. I think he is very wrong. I think if my hon. friend wants to learn the meaning and magic of words all he needs to do is listen a little more to the Prime Minister, and he will be able to preach the greatest sermon he ever dreamed about. But I said to my aunt, "Horseless means without a horse, does it not?" And she said, "Yes, Jim." I said, "Will it go without a horse?" And she said, "It will go without a horse." "Will it go up hill," I

Cooperative Commonwealth
asked. "Certainly it will go uphill," she replied. Then I said, "Well, I don't believe it, Aunt Laura; I don't believe it will go without a horse." Then we had that fairy tale about Cinderella and Prince Charming, and the glass carriage with the four horses. What have we to-day? We have a little instrument that has the power of sixty or a hundred horses.
What has capitalism done? It has ransacked the ages and spoiled the climes. It has solved the problem of production, and beyond the dreams of avarice, beyond any conception that any of us ever can have, the future will be even more glorious than the past.
Now look at the next section of this resolution. After starting on its way by stating what I claim to be a falsehood, it says that the capitalistic system should be superseded by a cooperative commonwealth in which the profit motive would be subordinated to that of public service. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre was a preacher of the gospel in which the ideal of unselfishness and public service was the keystone. For 1,935 years the Church of Jesus Christ has been alive in this world. The best educated, the most fearless and the best men we have are the priests and the preachers of our churches, but have the truths of the Christian religion penetrated to the core of society? Are they the dominating motives of men? Is unselfishness absolutely on the throne? Is it all powerful? How can we hope, by a resolution of this kind, to change the very nature of mankind? How can we hope, by dressing a criminal in a new suit of clothes, to make him a saint or a gentleman? How can it be done? Let us look at this problem from a philosophical standpoint. I have often wondered just why it was such good politics for a man to become a sort of socialist now and then.

Mr. Speaker, I was falling into the fatal error of looking at that jewel of truth and perceiving the wrong facet.

Let us go on with the resolution. We find in it the expression: "Ruthless competition replaced by collective ownership under democratic control". That is a mouthful. Is that communism? The resolution refers to ruthless competition which is to be replaced by collective ownership. The only collective ownership I could conceive would be ownership by the state. Does the expression "collective ownership" mean that the state shall own everything? And then we find the words "under democratic control". I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in referring to democratic control this afternoon said that this House of Commons, organized as it is, is incapable of realizing what he had hoped it would realize. What does he mean by democratic control? What does he mean by collective ownership? How is he going to attain collective ownership? Is there to be utter and immediate confiscation by the passage of law, so that all property shall be vested in the state? If there is not to be confiscation will there be payment for the property which the state will vest in itself? If there is to be payment, what kind of payment will it be? How much will the payment be, and in what way will it be paid? What does the resolution mean, anyway?
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the resolution, like all Oaul, is divided into three parts; but where one can find more gall in one part than in the other is very difficult for me to state-although I think it is in the first part.
I agree with the mover of the resolution when he states that the system under which we live is not an ideal system; but I ask him what is his alternative? What is the argument derived from history, and what do we learn from our contemporary experience? Let us analyze the situation in Germany to-day. Germany is a country which does its business under a greater degree of state control than obtains in any other country, with the exception of Russia. I read an article a short time ago in Current History stating that when one goes down the main street of Berlin he sees all the glory and all the pageantry of pre-war days, but if he should get off the main street he would find that the condition of the people is bad beyond description. In those side streets he would find families going out day after day to beg for their bread. That is an example of state control. Let us go back to Russia. The
(Mr. J H. Stitt.]
hon. member does not like me to refer to Russia; however I shall tell about a young man who came back from Russia to my constituency. This young Polish chap had learned to make tractors in Henry Ford's factory, and had been persuaded to go to Stalingrad to assist the Russians in the manufacture of automobiles. He was supplied with everything in the way of clothes and food, and was given adequate police protection. In the Chase National bank of New York $180 was placed each month to his credit. Notwithstanding all this he came back to the constituency of Selkirk to live with his peasant father and mother. Speaking to the boy directly-because I did not obtain my information from any intermediary source- I said, " Why did you come back to this country where no doubt some months will elapse before you can obtain a position? Why did you leave that new country with all the privileges it held for you?" He said, " Mr. Stitt, I was afraid to go outside the compound at night." "Why were you afraid?" I asked. He replied, " The Russians were so poorly clad I was afraid they would murder me for my clothes."
As it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
